position which Canada was taking at the recent international conference on the elimination of pollution from ships. Now that this large, international gathering in London, England, has completed its work, I would like to report progress. I would like to describe the results of this conference of flag states and coastal states, the main objective of which was to prevent the further deterioration of the world's oceans, seas and shipping lanes.
Oil was the only pollutant mentioned in the 1954 and 1969 conventions. The latest convention, that of 1973, includes toxic and suffocating substances other than oil. It includes white oils as well as black oils. It includes refined petroleum products as well as crude oil and bunker oil.
The new convention also contains important stipulations with regard to vessel construction. Segregated ballast will be required on all new tankers of more than 70,000 tons. The size of individual tanks in oil tankers is also limited so as to reduce the loss of oil from collisions and groundings in the future.
The right of coastal states to take action against a ship in trouble whicn also posed the threat of pollution to their shores has been expanded. Not only does it now cover dangerous substances other than oil, but it also extends this right to any distance which might reasonably be said to involve a threat or hazard to the territory of the coastal state.
With respect to other jurisdictional aspects of the convention an attempt was made at the conference to limit the right of enforcement of a coastal state to its territorial sea. This attempt was resisted successfully by Canada. The new convention adopts the compromise approach along the lines of the one negotiated at the London Dumping Conference in 1972 and allows a coastal state to enforce the convention "within its jurisdiction" without attempting to define how far that jurisdiction may extend. The convention thus recognizes that the nature and extent of coastal state jurisdiction as well as flag state jurisdiction may be changed as a result of the Law of the Sea Conference. Meanwhile it is open to a state to interpret the convention as permitting it to enforce its provisions in waters under its jurisdiction which, like fisheries closing lines, extend beyond its territorial sea.

Mr. Speaker, we won some and lost some. We failed, for example, to get approval of special preventative measures in special areas. The special areas we had in mind were those of exceptional ecological sensitivity whether they be inside, or outside the jurisdiction of the coastal state. We had our Arctic problem in mind. We were encouraged by the fact that a number of important flag states supported us. But the Canadian resolution failed to get the necessary two-thirds majority in the final plenary session of the conference. Needless to say, we will try again, but our next opportunity to deal with special areas is, at least, a few years away.
We also put forward the "port state enforcement concept" for the first time. In this we were strongly supported by the United States. Had it been accepted, violators of the convention could have been prosecuted in the ports of any contracting party regardless of where the offence took place and for up to three years after it occurred.
One of the defects of the 1954 convention is that violations which occur outside of the waters of the coastal state can only be dealt with by the flag state in which the ship is registered. The new convention beefs up the penalties but that is all. As a coastal state, Canada must continue to oppose this flag state regime and will, therefore, continue to press for "port state enforcement" at the Law of the Sea Conference in 1974.
Canada supported a United States proposal for the building of double bottoms in new oil tankers. This requirement was rejected by the conference as was the "sheen" concept which would have made it easier to prosecute ships trailing a thin sheen of oil. Instead of accepting the word of an officer of a coastal state, quantitative measures of loss of oil will still be needed in order to prosecute the ship which is responsible for pollution on the high seas.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I can say that the standards adopted by the latest IMCO conference are good, not excellent. In concept, they apply all around the world. But the conference did not adopt all of the measures which are necessary if they are to be enforced effectively by flag states and coastal states alike. We did not manage to deal with our special Arctic problem either.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment our delegation to the IMCO conference and especially its deputy head, Mr. E. G. Lee. It was very active. Anyone who was there will agree that it was one of the most influential delegations which we have sent abroad in recent years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in replying to the minister I think I should remind the House that in answer to the minister's statement on October 16 it was brought to the attention of the House that certain things which we should have been pursuing at this conference were neglected or omitted. This, of course, may have been because it was impossible to get them on the agenda. I refer to the fact that no matter what arrangements we make with respect to other nations we do need co-operation on international navigation standards. All the safeguards in the world are of no account if vessels are

operating under navigational standards that allow collisions.
There has been no mention by the minister today, nor was there on October 16, of international arrangements for co-operation in the clean-up of oil. Again I stress that compensation is no comfort to those on shores that are befouled by oil.
I again remind the government that, in order to achieve the other objectives the minister has stated still remain to be achieved, our own moral position must be first rate. I refer to the fact that we have had an inconsistent policy of complaining about oil tankers on the west coast and taking almost no action on the east coast.
On page two of the statement which the minister kindly delivered to me just before the House met he says:
The right of coastal states to take action against a ship in trouble which also posed the threat of pollution to its shores has been expanded. Not only does it now cover dangerous substances other than oil, but it also extends this right to any distance which might reasonably be said to involve a threat or hazard to the territory of the coastal state.
This is all very well but, as has been demonstrated by recent spills on the west coast, in this country we do not have the equipment nor the trained men to deal adequately with minor spills that are taking place in our own harbours. Acquiring the right to contain spills farther out to sea does us little good if we do not have the men and material to do so. The minister is aware of this problem as he comes from a riding bordering the very harbour that has recently been the subject of two spills. I would ask the minister and other members of the government to take this into account.
The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) referred to this matter on October 16. He said that we must be prepared to take unilateral action in cases where a convention or agreement is lacking. This party endorses the position taken by the hon. member for Skeena on October 16. We have already taken such action, as he pointed out, with respect to the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act, an area that is very special to us. The fact that we may not be able to get agreement at this time should not in any way detract from our determination to act unilaterally when our self-interest is at stake.
I notice with a great deal of gratification that the minister said in his statement:
The new convention declares that the Mediterranean Sea, Black Sea, Baltic Sea, Red Sea and the gulfs area including the Sea of Oman are designated as special areas-
Speaking as one who not many months ago had occasion to be swimming in the Mediterranean at Tel Aviv, I can assure hon. members that this prohibition of oil spills was long overdue. Anyone who swims in those waters will testify to the fact that as you swim you move globules of oil out of the way. That is no exaggeration.
We shall face these problems along our coasts unless we are prepared to take unilateral action if required and to see to it that our efforts in years to come to obtain international co-operation are made with the necessary thrust. I might add that I would have been pleased, as I know other members from the west coast would have been, if the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Puget Sound had

Even though I have been able to give the statement only cursory examination, I do not think the minister should be very proud of it, because it does not accomplish a great deal in terms of pollution control or with regard to the environmental concerns of the people of this land.
I want to say at the outset that I certainly welcome the position taken by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) in endorsing the concept of unilateral action which we have advocated as being most necessary for a long period of time. I would like to hear the leader of his party make that declaration so we would know where the party stands as well as the member for Vancouver South.
What we sought to do at the IMCO conference and what this statement indicates we did do was to subject the position of Canada to the decision of 90 other nations. By
Pollution from Ships
participating in this conference and giving up our position and rights we are in effect letting the other nations of the world decide what Canada is going to do to preserve its integrity and its environment and to control pollution. In the whole course of relationships between nations, changes have been made in international law by unilateral decision of one or a number of countries pushing and forcing an issue. Canada has moved away from that course and is willing to go along with what the flag states want to see accomplished, not what is of value to Canada.
In his statement the minister said Canada failed to get approval of special preventative measures in special areas. To clarify that, he said he was talking about the Arctic-area of this nation. This means that when the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act was presented to the House four or five years ago the government was just engaging in a windowdressing program and the act is nothing more than a bunch of words on paper. As the minister said, it means nothing. We attempted to get some consideration of the question of Arctic waters when we have laws on the statute books to deal with it and we failed. The minister went on to say that another opportunity to raise this matter is a few years away. I consider this to be another indication of a sellout of the interests of Canada by this government, especially with regard to the question of oil pollution.
It is regrettable that there was no reference in the statement to special waters of concern to us in British Columbia such as the Strait of Juan de Fuca and the Gulf of Georgia. There is no indication of the government's intention with regard to the critical situation that has developed in one instance and may well develop again in connection with the Cherry Point refinery in the state of Washington. This omission indicates that the government does not have any measures to deal with that. The minister said in his statement:
Canada supported a United States proposal for the building of double bottoms in new oil tankers.
I was surprised to hear that. A week before the minister went to the IMCO conference in London he raked me over the coals because I said Canada was taking a neutral position by not saying anything about double hull vessels, and I draw a distinction between double hull and double bottom vessels. At that time the minister said in no way would he or the government have anything to do with supporting the concept of double hulls for tankers because that would only have value if the tanker ran aground on a soft and not a rocky bottom. A week before the conference the minister was arguing against the necessity of seeing that oil tankers plying the waters of the world were built with double hulls. Now he turns around and says he supported a United States proposal for the building ol' double bottoms in new oil tankers, indicating that it is probably not double bottoms he is concerned about but double talk.

Mr. Speaker, that we should always be provided with copies of ministers' statements only some four minutes before two o'clock is regrettable. This is readily understandable. We must complete a thorough review or study of the last arguments within seconds if we want to make relevant observations on these statements.
However, the minister's statement shows one thing: we have tried mainly to be good diplomats instead of being statesmen who are able to represent truly the attitude of Canada towards other countries and to make suggestions which may be nationalistic but which would really protect the Canadian coastline.
On page 3, it is stated that seas like the Mediterranean, the Black Sea, the Baltic, the Red Sea and the areas around gulfs, including the Oman Sea, are special areas. And, the ridiculous thing is that the large ships are not allowed to dump or spill oil, but the small ships are allowed to do it. But the damage caused by two or three small ships to equivalent to that caused by one large ship. We then beat about the bush without taking any specific position. I suspect that there may be somewhat acrid discussions between the government of Quebec and that of Ottawa concerning the pollution possibility of the St. Lawrence, for example, especially when no clear position is taken on pollution and that any coastal state has merely the possibility of taking such positions and perhaps prosecuting a boat which will have damaged its coasts.
On the whole, we can surely congratulate those who have shown satisfactory diplomacy, but we cannot congratulate the government for a realistic national attitude about the protection of the environment as well as that of the Canadian coasts.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In view of the fact the National Energy Board has received certain alternative proposals- not applications but proposals-relating to construction of an oil pipeline to Montreal and that any further action on these proposals by Interprovincial is contingent upon a clear statement of policy from the minister on the need for such pipeline as well as a statement of intent to assure an oil supply for the pipeline, would the minister inform the House whether he has made a clear statement as to the need for the pipeline and a clear statement of assurance regarding oil supply for such a pipeline, and if so, for what size of pipeline?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PROPOSED OIL PIPELINE EXTENSION TO MONTREAL- AVAILABILITY OF SUPPLY-APPROVAL BY QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the basic question of whether or not there should be a pipeline, that was indeed determined in principle by the government in September. The critical questions at this point are the financial circumstances under which the pipeline would be constructed by Interprovincial Pipe Line Company, the extent to which for security purposes additional capacity would be built into the line and, therefore, who should bear the cost, and how the line would fit in with the special plans the province of Quebec has in this regard.
My understanding from the board and from my officials is that there have been discussions on these points with the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company, as indeed there have been discussions with the Quebec authorities. I regret that I cannot announce anything more definitive regarding these terms, but my understanding is that negotiations are advancing.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, under the National Energy Board Act the board has responsibility with regard to gas and with regard to oil to make certain that no exports shall take place unless they are surplus to Canadian requirements. Obviously the decision with regard to construction of a pipeline into Montreal would add the Montreal market to Canadian requirements, and under those circumstances this would be at the expense of any exports that we might have under way. It is anticipated that over a period of time stretching up to ten years there would be a reduction in the export component, and this would be one of the aspects that would be involved in that consideration. The time span of approximately two years that would precede the actual operation of the pipeline would be notice to United States users that they should make other arrangements for supply once the decision is made to go ahead.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to my recollection, the issues agitating the voters during the last election, in my riding at any rate, were law and order, pollution controls, and foreign investment policy. These are all important issues and the voters were right to have them in the forefront of their minds.
The present government chose to disregard prevailing public opinion with respect to law and order when it introduced Bill C-2. It has done little to take effective measures with regard to pollution control, particularly with respect to tanker routes. Now, we have a foreign take-over bill, as it is called, which is an attempt to control and regulate certain aspects of foreign investment in Canada. What does this offer, Mr. Speaker? Further, in what manner should we accept this offer?
It has been clear to me for a long time that we, in Canada, must do something to secure for Canadians a greater share in the making of decisions which affect the economic activities of this country. Much has been made of the need to obtain a greater share of the equity capital of enterprises operating in this country. Like many other Canadians, it has been my policy to direct my investments along these lines. I have done what little I could, with the excess capital I had for investment, to make sure that what I had was going into the development of Canada through the development of Canadian business and enterprise. If you like, you can call me a nut for insisting on taking this sort of course and not investing in a way that would bring the best economic return. Perhaps I have not been seeking the best economic return. By the same token, you could call several hundred thousand fellow Canadians nuts because we did not calculate in terms of dollars and cents when we put on uniforms some 34 years ago.
By insisting on my investment policy, I have not always gained the maximum return; however, I have always felt, and I still feel, that my return was not really to be calculated in those terms, but, rather, in terms of my helping to promote Canadianism, whether economic or in our political life. The bill before us does nothing to encourage Canadians to follow this practice. Unfortunately, there are some who feel that we must convert economic patriotism, if you like, into a profitable attitude. This aspect of foreign investment deserves much more attention than it is now getting.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), for example, ought to provide financial inducements to Canadian investors, individual and corporate, by which they will invest more frequently and more heavily in Canadian enterprises. The bill before us makes no attempt to deal with this aspect of investment in Canadian enterprise, and I maintain that therein lies one of its major defects.
Having said that and judging from my own experience, I say that assurance of Canadian equity capital, particularly by individuals, in Canadian companies is not an absolute guarantee of effective Canadian control of those companies. How many of those, in this House owning voting shares in Canadian companies, exercise their voting privileges regularly? Let's be honest now. How many exercise
November 6, 1973

them regularly? And how many have ever exercised them? Is it not more often your experience that you proceed by proxy or perhaps even by default?
In saying this I do not belittle the value of the incentives for encouraging Canadians to invest in Canadian enterprise. The operations are Canadian; the proceeds come back to Canadians by way of dividends, share options and so on. It becomes more fully a Canadian operation to the extent that this process is carried on with the involvement of and to the benefit of Canadians.
I suggest, therefore, that one of the things Canadians are looking for at this moment is something this bill does not really provide. We are looking for something which, if my knowledge of parliamentary practice is correct, the opposition cannot supply when the government fails to do so, namely, changes in the income tax law which would encourage Canadians to invest in Canadian enterprises and to make it profitable for them to do so. This is a governmental prerogative. I would say, however, that if my party has any hand in the preparation of the next budget, and I have a sneaking hunch we may very well have, you can bet your bottom dollar that I will be arguing this course on my Minister'of Finance. I have some reason to believe he will heed that sort of advice.
