This bill is defective in a lot of other ways. We have a number of amendments on the order paper, many of them directed toward ensuring greater federal-provincial consultation. The present government, I am sure, will protest violently when I come to my next sentence, but in anticipation of that protest I would just like to say that to organize meetings and enter into dialogue is not to be confused with consultation. It is my contention that, and here it comes, the present government has failed abominably in the area of federal-provincial consultation. It held a Western Economic Opportunities Conference, but what was achieved beyond the fact that federal and provincial ministers met face to face? How much provincial concern was absorbed by the federal government? How much of it was stored up for use when the need arose? What assessments were made of the areas of provincial requirements and the need, on occasion, to get on the phone and talk to the minister involved when crises blow up?
We saw an instance last week of a blatant disregard of a legitimate and understandable concern of a provincial government. This was to be found in the statement made here last Thursday on the energy question by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald). The Alberta ministers directly responsible in the Alberta government for the provinces' resources, including supplies of energy-producing products, gas and oil, were in Ottawa on the Monday and spent nearly all day with the federal minister. I do not know what they talked about at that day long meeting. I was not there. These discussions were private. However, I would be greatly surprised if the federal minister did not get the following message communicated to him in one form or another, either directly which I think most likely, or indirectly. The message must
Foreign Investment Review Act have been put across. Why else, I feel bound to ask, did the Alberta ministers bother to come to Ottawa?
The message that must have been put across would probably read as follows: "Look, we are heading for trouble as a result of the Middle East oil crisis. For Pete's sake, if you have to do anything on the spur of the moment to deal with that situation as it affects Canada, give one or the other of us a call, talk to us; let us know what it is you have in mind to say or do. Let us consult about it. We have had some experience, after all, in producing and seeing to the distribution of hydrocarbons in the energy field, so don't do anything, we implore you, without first getting a reading from us. We have quite substantial supplies. Maybe between us we can get things worked out with the minimum of dislocation all around." That, I firmly believe, is one of the messages the federal minister ought to have received from the Albertans when they were here on Monday of last week. They may not have put it in those terms, but being reasonable men and staunch upholders of Canadianism, they are certain to have left an impression of that sort.
That meeting, let us remember, was on Monday, October 29. Ten days earlier, in the House, in reply to a question put to him by the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and others relating to a federal pricing policy for oil, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources had us all believing that his department was thinking in terms of letting the price of crude oil in Canada be determined on the basis of a formula having, as its principal ingredient, the price of offshore oil arriving in Montreal. That formula, we were given to understand, while not the best price available to Albertan oil producers, would meet their requirements and would satisfy Alberta and formed part of the government's energy policy. Within those limits it seemed possible that the Canadian product would be suitably priced, not to everyone's satisfaction, but as a result of the best option open.
This element, we might have thought, would have figured rather prominently in the statement on energy the minister felt obliged to make last Thursday. And what did we find? We had a bombshell dropped on us in the House in the form of an almost 400 per cent increase in the export tax on oil, without any attempt on the minister's part to mention domestic price levels and still less to have any real consultations with Alberta when the crunch came. Little surprise, then, that the Alberta government is aggrieved.
This is what I mean when I say this government refuses to consult the provinces on matters affecting provincial responsibilities. No one can have confidence in the undertakings which have been given during recent debates that the government would consult the province; those undertakings have to be written into the law. It is for this reason that this particular defect in the bill must be remedied by the passage of one of the various amendments put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay).
This government cannot be trusted to administer Bill C-132, as it now stands, should it be passed into law. We have cause for concern because of past experience, and I have gone to great lengths to explain that experience and our misgivings. This government seems determined to

November 6, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act antagonize the provinces rather than consult with them on matters over which they have a dominating interest and, in some instances, jurisdiction.
There is another grave defect in this bill. It deals with only two aspects of the investment of foreign capital, the take-over of an existing enterprise, which will be refused by the agency unless it can be shown that the take-over would be likely to result in a substantial benefit to Canada. The determination of "substantial benefit to Canada" is going to be difficult enough to define as the bill was originally drafted. Even taking into account the industrial and economic policies enunciated by the province in which the enterprise is to be carried on, and enlisting provincial collaboration in doing so as suggested in the amendment submitted by my colleague from Central Nova, there will still be no easy way to define "substantial benefit" to everyone's satisfaction, that is as far as take-overs and new investments are concerned.
The second feature of this bill is the attempt to subject new capital to controls like those imposed on take-over bids. Again, we have the problem of defining with any assurance of success "substantial benefit of Canada". There is, however, an additional area which the bill does not touch. It is the one which I think caused a great deal of concern, heartburn and misgiving during the past election. This is one which caused a great deal of heartburn and misgiving during the last election. It is a great oversight and a dangerous loophole which must be plugged, if not by this bill then by some other legislation. It relates to expansion or diversification of existing foreign-financed enterprises. These should be considered very carefully.
A foreign-financed enterprise which is already operating in Canada or which manages to get itself accepted as a new enterprise here may set its sights on a Canadian-owned and operated enterprise already in being. No names, no pack-drill, Mr. Speaker, but one can think of plenty of illustrations. The initial entry into Canada may, indeed, have been obtained for the express purpose of getting into a position to increase the power base in Canada, and not necessarily in the same field of activity; perhaps it is merely to diversify holdings, spread risks- oil into publishing, manufacturing into resource development or even into running a chain of retail stores.
The legislation before us makes no attempt to regulate or control such a form of activity. It is not, therefore, entirely satisfactory. It fails to respond to the increasingly vocal demands one hears in favour of regaining control of our own affairs. It is a start, and that is all-at least it is a start provided some of the defects to which I have referred can be remedied. Otherwise, it is not likely to be a very effective instrument. In fact, even with our amendments, it would be a clumsy one. I commend those amendments to all hon. members none the less, because without them we shall see another bureaucratic monster in our midst.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address the House briefly today on the particular subject before us and on the needs of the Canadian people. I would like to put the matter in the context of our present

situation and the challenges which currently face us. Too often, perhaps, we look at these issues in terms of ideology; we consider legislation in terms of situations which existed a decade or even longer ago.
One of the starting points one might take is that of determining our position with respect to the control of energy in this country, more particularly in the field of oil products. One might ask oneself, what is the basic function of government in this area. Surely, the first charge upon any government of a community, whether it be a municipality, a province or a nation, is to see that the basic needs of the people who live in that community are served-to see that the people have shelter, food and a workable social relationship with each other so that they can live together. These are minimum requirements. A government must conduct its affairs so that this responsibility is discharged.
The energy question is one of the real challenges which face us today. We have left this field to foreign-owned concerns to the extent that some 90 per cent of our resources are controlled by people other than Canadians. The companies concerned are not charged with serving the needs of Canadians. It is true that a National Energy Board has been set up, and that it is charged with ensuring that certain guidelines are observed. But they are minimum guidelines. Other than this, we have left the field to private corporations-multinational corporations for the most part-in the assumption that Canada would be well served.
One watershed was reached, in my opinion, when we decided to build a trans-Canada pipeline. That was the occasion for one of the great debates in this chamber. It was so important that a book was written about it setting out what happened at the time of the debate-the position taken by various parties and individuals and the final outcome. The book set out the roles played. It dealt with the activities of the Murchisons, the great Texas promoters and other oil operators. It also included the role of the late C.D. Howe who was quite properly dubbed minister of everything in the Liberal government of the day. I say this was a watershed, a point of decision in the affairs of this country. Canada decided at that time to leave the oil component of its energy resources in the hands of independent ownership, or private enterprise. It was assumed that by so doing the community would be well served and that consumers would be comfortable and secure. Mr. Speaker, if there is any assumption which has been proven wrong, that one has been proven wrong and it has taken less than 25 years to do so.
The government across the way comes now to the House timidly and hesitantly with a bill which seeks to limit the free rein enjoyed by private enterprise and multinational corporations. It seeks timidly and hesitantly to ensure that the country may be able to protect its own interests and that some government, not necessarily this one but any Canadian government, may be able to take sufficient legislative action as to enable it to control effectively the affairs of the nation and protect the interests of its citizens. The bill before us will not do that. It will not enable the government to control the affairs of the nation effectively. We have reached a point at which we do not exercise effective control, a point at which we find our-
November 6, 1973

selves entirely without a policy which will meet the needs of the times. We are in a position where .one level of government quarrels with another over what to do about the resources which are necessary to provide the heat and power this country needs. The tragedy of it all is that neither we nor the province of Alberta any longer owns the essential resources. These resources have been alienated from our control, and this has happened with our consent. If this measure before the House proposes to do anything, its first objective should be no longer to tolerate the alienation of our resources and our power. Although this may be necessary at times in manufacturing, we should not tolerate the basic resources of this country being wrenched from the control of the Canadian people.
Let me give another example. A few years ago we wanted to ship some grain to the People's Republic of China, which since that time we have recognized. However, at the time the People's Republic of China was one of the bad boys of the world as far as the United States was concerned, so the United States declared that none of the United States companies would be allowed to ship Canadian grain to China. I recall that we needed certain equipment to unload the grain boats when they reached Chinese Ports and the U.S. government even sought to prevent us from using that equipment. But the reason we were able to proceed to export the grain we wanted to export was that the Canadian co-operatives happened to own the most important grain forwarding and grain storage company in Canada.
I suspect that the only reason we owned and controlled at that time, as we still do, 75 per cent to 90 per cent of the grain handling facilities in the prairie regions is that they were co-operative facilities. Had they been privately owned, the chances are they would have belonged to the United States corporations or some other foreign country. In this instance the people, through the co-operatives, owned the facilities. The Canadian Wheat Board, which was and is a Crown corporation, was then in operation. This grain was our product; we had the physical facilities to move and market the grain, and we did so. Had we not been in that position we would not have been able to decide our own destiny at that time.
If any member of this House wants to read a very interesting chapter in the history of grain, then I suggest he read about the U.S.S.R. buying over 400 million bushels of U.S. wheat, about one-third of the crop, from private corporations in the United States. This was a purchase subsidized by the U.S. government with the full complicity of the private grain companies in the U.S., a deal that cost the U.S. taxpayers some millions of dollars. The companies involved included Carghill, Dreyfus, Bunge; it reads like a list of the mighty corporations and makes for fascinating reading.
To complete each deal, the company or corporation concerned would contact the U.S. department of agriculture and ask whether the subsidy and guarantees were still in force. When they received confirmation that they were, they proceeded with the sale, committing the U.S. government and people to millions of dollars, to the benefit of a foreign government. If anyone wants an example of the operation, let them read the story of the amber fields of
Foreign Investment Review Act grain, a record of the consciences of the multinational corporations and the consciences of the rich.
This is a mighty nation that I refer to, Mr. Speaker. It is not Canada, a country of some 20 million people; this is the mightiest nation in the world with over 200 million people, sovereign in its own right; a country whose mighty navy roams the seas and whose army calls the shots. The U.S.S.R., with the help of the multinational corporations moved in and took that country to the cleaners. The result was an increase in the price of food and feed grain, and an increase in the cost of production and of food from which this whole continent still suffers. The principal reason for this was that the United States of America had no real control over the movement and sale of its primary foodstuffs; it had no co-ordinated surveillance over its primary sources of food.
In this country we have. Through the co-operative grain companies that we have built, and through the Canadian Wheat Board, we do have a very large measure of control. What I am saying is that the multinational companies which handle grain did the same thing to the United States food supply that they are now doing to our petroleum supply, and to the supply of heating oil that we in this country are going to need this coming winter. There are two developed countries in our world that have adequate supplies of energy. One is the U.S.S.R.; the other is Canada. The minister in charge of energy in this country stood in the House last night and told Canadian citizens they may be cold in the coming winter. He told them to turn down their thermostats and to switch off their lights. Is this a reflection of an organized community? I suggest it is a shame and disgrace to the Canadian people, and is a reflection on those who have controlled the destiny of this nation up to the present time.
What have we in the way of an agency that could go to sources of energy, even outside our own country, perhaps the Middle East or Venezuela, with the authority to say that we are ready to purchase "X" number of barrels of oil, asking for a firm contract? I suggest that we have no such agency. All we have is a joker associated with the refinery at Come By Chance who appears on television, and he did so last night, suggesting that the Canadian government wants us to sell the refinery products to the United States. That individual does nothing more than make suggestions, while men like Shaheen spend $400,000 chartering the Queen Elizabeth to move from a port in the United States to Canada for the purpose of putting on a big party. I should like to know at whose expense that party was thrown. I suggest that, eventually, the expense will be borne by the Canadian taxpayer. I suppose we will be asked to switch off a few lights in order to save energy.
I fully expected the minister across the aisle to rise in his place to say that we have a program which will assure supplies to meet the needs of Canadians. Certainly, we could expect the minister to say that if this program could not be put into effect within three months the government had positive plans to put it into effect within six months or a year. Surely, we should have some indication that the government plans to institute a program under the authority of those responsible for resources in Canada. These resources should be put at the disposal of a Crown

November 6, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act corporation or some agency in order to meet the needs of the Canadian people, but that is not the case. We stand in this Chamber debating this bill and talking about whether we will actually have control of our natural resources. We have talked for some time about the establishment of a Canadian policy which would ensure the future destiny and welfare of Canada.
It is time that we abandoned this wavering position, as illustrated by this bill, and got down to fundamentals. I suggest we must do so before it is too late. We must make a move in the direction of Canadian ownership of Canadian resources. We must do so very quickly in order that we obtain the confidence of Canadian people that we will be able to meet the needs of Canadians in the future.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
I am mindful of the problem of foreign domination of Canadian industry and the problem of achieving economic independence for Canada. These problems deserve serious consideration and a wise and effective legislative response. Canada's economic growth and development has depended greatly on foreign investment and it is an essential element in the future growth of many parts of our country. A national policy defining and clarifying the role of foreign investment in Canada is needed if many important decisions relating to this country's economic life are not to be made outside of Canada by non-Canadians and, if in fact, such decisions are to be in our best interests. Fundamental to any such approach is a clearly stated national policy setting out a long-term economic development strategy designed to preserve the economic and political independence of Canada and which will have adequate regard for our very serious problems of regional disparity.
There is no question that Canadians look forward to playing a growing role in Canadian development and economic management. It is no wonder that Canadians view with concern the fact that over one-half of the corporations operating in our country are non-resident owned, and the extremely high percentage of foreign ownership reflected in manufacturing industries concerned with rubber products, petroleum, chemicals and chemical products, primary metals and electrical products. Of equal concern to Canadians is the fact that foreign investors receive a large portion of the grants under special and incentive programs and continue to use Canadian money to expand foreign ownership in the Canadian economy.
Bill C-132, the foreign investment review bill, now before us, seeking to rectify these problems, is essentially a negative document concerned with control of foreign investment in existing and new industries without at the same time dealing with positive measures to ensure the survival and expansion of Canadian companies. It fails to increase Canadian presence in existing subsidiaries within this country or to provide measures for making Canadian capital available to those individuals and enterprises willing and able to make constructive use of Canadian resources and manpower. Canadian risk capital has not been encouraged to match Canadian opportunities and entrepreneurial talent. It is unfortunate that the government has been unable to grasp this concept.
The bill also fails to establish clear standards of good corporate behaviour for the foreign-owned or controlled enterprise.

The government should act in co-operation with the provinces to establish and define key categories of business, and strategic sectors of the economy, which are to be considered reserved for Canadian ownership, for controlled minor foreign participation, or for Canadian development. Clearly, it is imperative that our federal and provincial governments should meet and discover areas in the structure of our natural resources that should be reserved for development in Canada by Canadians and for Canadians. The amount and degree of foreign investment, if any, in these areas should be determined.
There is, I believe, an area in which provincial governments might be encouraged to protect recreational lands around lakes and streams by holding them in the public domain for the use of all our people.
The government must move positively to provide incentives through the tax system to encourage increased investment by Canadians in Canadian firms. The government should move positively, and in concert with the provinces, to encourage and assist businessmen and schools of business administration to provide more extensive and appropriate programs in order to enlarge the pool of entrepreneurial and managerial talent in Canada. In developing the financial institutions required to match Canadian capital with Canadian opportunity and entrepreneurial talent the government should take positive measures to divert financial assistance to new firms in key sectors of the economy to help them import technology and management contracts.
The province of New Brunswick is still in need of external capital in large amounts to provide jobs and opportunities for Canadians living in that province. Indeed, Canadians in New Brunswick are entitled to the assurance that their capital needs will be met, and will not be unduly delayed or hindered by the operation of the foreign investment review agency set up by this bill. New Brunswick is dependent to a great degree on investment from outside to develop new projects and assist in the expansion of existing firms. New Brunswick agencies have tried to attract investment capital to New Brunswick and, since 1970, of 76 projects producing employment for 3,382 persons, about 50 per cent of the capital invested and 40 per cent of the total jobs created were a direct result of investment from outside the province.
In my opinion, this bill must be improved to ensure that provincial points of view will be adequately protected. Without adequate provincial input, the ponderous considerations of the bureaucrats in the foreign investment review agency may result in costly delays, uncertainty and a diminution in the badly needed investment in New Brunswick. There is little in this bill, or indeed in the government's total program, to illustrate positive programs that are put forward to assure that Canadians will be encouraged to save and invest, and that vehicles will be developed to divert adequate savings to the needs of New Brunswick and other slow growth areas, in a manner that will not be contradictory to the national interest.
In short, the government's foreign investment proposals contribute little to increased Canadian participation and/or Canadian ownership in the Canadian economy. We are faced with a relatively negative bill that has the
November 6, 1973

potential of aggravating the already serious disparities that exist between regions of this country.
Despite the factors set out in the bill which the foreign investment review agency must consider in determining what is in the national interest, the lack of a properly evaluated criterion leaves the agency with outrageously large areas of personal judgment. Some of my colleagues have indicated amendments to strengthen and correct these guidelines, and I am inclined to favour them.
In the administration of this measure, it is imperative that the government recognize that this is essentially a nation of five regions; that our national policies must be flexible enough to give maximum protection to one or two segments without exploiting the others. New Brunswick's bitter experience in monetary, fiscal, energy, transportation and tariff policies is a cause for concern. We in New Brunswick need a comprehensive program to increase Canadian participation in our economy, revisions to the Bank Act and the development of measures to encourage investment of risk capital. This bill alone, without amendments, will not do the job. Even the Canada Development Corporation, if given an expanded role with regional guidelines, can do much to make a positive contribution to the situation, and so too can a requirement that foreign firms make voting shares available to Canadians.
As for New Brunswick, I believe that massive investment is absolutely necessary if we are to progress. I believe that foreign investors should be sought and, provided they become good corporate citizens, be welcomed to our midst as Canadians. A comprehensive approach to national development indicating the acceptable role foreign capital can play is an essential element in the orderly development and growth of Canada. It is in search of this goal that I have attempted to set out some factors to be considered if we are to evoke an effective and comprehensive legislative response.
I have attempted to emphasize the benefits that can accrue to the slower growth regions of Canada with such a positive approach to the problems of economic and political independence while also indicating the hardship that will surely follow from the strictly administered negative approach which now exists in this bill, and which I hope will be expanded and improved by amendments contemplated by my colleagues. The minister can commence the positive approach by giving his assurance that New Brunswick in particular, and all slow growth regions of Canada, will not suffer for want of risk capital because of the provisions of this bill.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly on the amendments proposed to this bill. It is a matter of record that for a long time our party has been concerned about the growing influence of foreign investment in Canada. It is equally a matter of record that the Canadian people are deeply concerned about the effect of that growing influence on their daily problems, such as the cost of living and problems of this nature. People are worried about where we are heading as a nation. It is the purpose of this bill to provide a screening agency to review, assess and control the extent and
Foreign Investment Review Act influence of foreign investment in Canada. In the words of the bill itself;
.. . the ability of Canadians to maintain effective control over their economic environment is a matter of national concern,
I stress the phrase "a matter of national concern". So far as the extent of foreign investment is concerned, that is a matter of record and I will not expend a great amount of time quoting statistics to indicate the extent of that foreign investment. What I would like to comment upon is the nature of the influence of foreign investment on our country, because it seems to me that an understanding of that influence is basic in considering the amendments that are before us today, and indeed for an understanding of the need for the control of foreign investment in Canada as is laid out in the bill.
The growing influence of multinational corporations is twofold in that it is both economic and political in its effect. It would be a grievous error to conclude that the over extension of foreign investment in Canada endangers our economy only because it deprives Canadians of the ownership of their own industries. It has this effect, of course, with the result that there is a steady drain of Canadian dollars to foreign countries, and in particular to the United States.
Some people are fond of extolling the benefits of foreign investment in our country. They say it brings us jobs, it brings us industries. But the figures tell us that between 1960 and 1969 we lost $2 billion more than we gained through foreign investment, and I cannot for the life of me see how this can be construed to be an advantage. Only last year, dividend interest in foreign owned businesses was exported to the tune of $2.35 billion. In nearly every paper you pick up, there is growing evidence of more and more take-overs of our industries. As early as 1969, which is not too long ago, the Financial Post began an editorial in this fashion:
Clearly, time is running out as far as Canada's independence is concerned. The sweep of foreign (particularly U S.) control of industry and resources in Canada is not matched in any other industrial country.
But we cannot separate the economic influence from the inevitable political influence of such corporate giants on the affairs of the nations which they invade. Corporate giants such as ITT are multinational only in the sense that they exist in various nations, but as Professor Papandreou pointed out in a recent article in the Canadian Forum, the term "multinational" obscures the fact that such corporations are basically ethnocentric, that is that they operate essentially from their country of origin and that their influence emanates essentially from their country of origin. An American corporation does not become Canadian by the mere device of tacking "Canadian" in front of its name, as in the case, for example, of Canadian General Electric.
Corporate systems, when they become large enough, become instruments of foreign policy of their base country just as in reverse, the base country uses its influence abroad to further the interests of the corporate system. The activities of ITT in Chile are an example of this mutual co-operation between corporation and state. We are concerned in Canada at this moment with a threatened

November 6, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act fuel shortage, and whether we freeze or not this winter lies largely in the hands of foreign-based oil corporations.
The point that I am trying to make, therefore, is that our consideration of the amendments before us should be directed toward strengthening the control of Canadians over the development of their economic resources and to strengthen at the same time their political independence which must, of necessity, be eroded as foreign domination of our economy increases. Make no mistake about it, political influence is the bed partner of economic influence.
The problem of politico-economic domination of our country is of national concern, and that national concern should override regional differences. For this reason, I would oppose any amendment that has the effect of hamstringing the work of the proposed foreign investment review agency. I am thinking in particular of an amendment such as amendment No. 5 in the name of the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) which reads:
In any case where a review or assessment of a proposed or actual investment is likely to affect significantly a province or provinces, a recommendation to the minister thereon shall be submitted by a panel of officers of whom a majority shall be representative of such province or provinces.
If we accept the threat of foreign control, political or economic, of huge multinational corporations then we must rise above consideration of regional differences, and thing together as Canadians in order to regain this country for Canadians. Amendments such as the one I have just quoted place the concern of a particular area over the national concern. Such an amendment places a stumbling block in the way of effective action toward the end visualized by the bill itself, because every measure taken will be subject to agreement, in an area where history shows agreement is the exception rather than the rule.
If Bill C-132 is effectively legislated and administered, it may help protect the interests of the Canadian people as a whole. It is a responsibility of this parliament as a whole to ensure that the government does take effective action to give Canadians some measure of control over their own destinies.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on rising to take part in this debate, I must first mention the title of the bill, which is an act to establish an agency for the control of foreign investment. Very few pieces of legislation come before this House that are more acceptable in concept. Today, everybody in Canada wants to do something about controlling foreign investment, and the power that foreign investment may have over Canadian lives.
I well remember the former bagman for the Liberal party in Alberta, now a member of the other place, Senator Hays, who also became a minister of agriculture, in a speech in Calgary saying that what we should have was economic union with the United States. I abhorred the thought. I wondered what kind of reasoning it was, but somehow it is the reasoning of some very wealthy people in Canada. They want economic union with the United States. I have never been one of them, but after looking at this bill I have some questions to put to the minister. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie)

is an obliging person. He is always willing to help. But sometimes in his eagerness to help he may harm, and I am a little worried about that in the present case. There may be harmful parts in this legislation. I can support the over-all concept but, as I say, the remarks of the Alberta senator in Calgary were very much against my general train of thought.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Nelson) said we must put aside our regional beliefs, and rise above that plateau. Those are strange remarks for one coming from British Columbia. I always thought that the mountains created a natural barrier. Whenever I crossed that barrier I found that the people behind it engaged in individualistic thinking. I think the hon. member's dream is a little pious, a little bit hopeful. All of us are not perfect. All of us have been sent to Ottawa to represent our constituencies and regions. We want to make certain that our constituencies and regions develop, believing that, as they develop, so grows Canada.
I well remember during the last election the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), who is in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, saying the government would do something about Vancouver, that it would spend some money there to develop the port. I only point this out to show how we are all determined to help our. own regions. Those in power have a record which shows they help their own regions rather than others. I will go on to prove that record, Mr. Speaker. That is why I support the amendment before us calling for regional representation when hearing the various applications.
I had placed a question on the order paper asking how much money had been spent by the government on the various ports throughout Canada during the last five years. I selected the period of five years because that covers the time since the government took office. In 1967, the federal government spent something like $17 million on the port of Vancouver. Each year from 1967 to 1972 this amount dropped off, until it reached $6 million or $7 million in 1972. I might add that Vancouver is the largest port in Canada. It handles 27 per cent of all tonnage entering and leaving Canada.
I thought it strange that the Minister of Justice should come out to Calgary during the election campaign and say the government would spend more money on the port of Vancouver. But on looking at the answer to my question I found a reason. The next largest port in Canada happens to be Montreal. It handles 17 per cent of the total tonnage entering and leaving Canada. Five years ago $19 million was spent on it, and in 1972 $20 million, showing that expenditures there held level. This indicated that some regional preference was shown.
One can point to different regional pressures that have been brought to bear on the government. Walter Stewart in his book "Divide and Con" has pointed out the regional pressures that develop. In case somebody has not read it, I would quote from page 160 as follows:
A $10.3 million park at Mont Sainte Anne, twenty-five miles north of Quebec City, in Liberal Montmorency riding.
A $16 million national historical park in the heart of Jean Marchand's Quebec City riding . . .
A $30 million eighty-six acre park on the Toronto lakefront. . .
November 6, 1973

Those are example of regional pressure. I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) exercised some regional pressure with respect to the Toronto project.
A senior citizens' home for Port Hawkesbury, also in Allan MacEachen's riding ....
A $30 million dock for Mulgrave, Nova Scotia, which also just happens to be in Allan MacEachen's riding.
There was a little regional pressure there.
The author of this book is not a political person. In fact, I think he says in other books that he is a believer in the NDP philosophy. On page 61 he writes:
. .. my vote goes to Jean Marchand, the Minister, as he then was, of Regional Economic Expansion. Who else would put out a colour brochure listing the $270 million in federal grants pumped into his own area since 1967? Who else would put up a billboard to proclaim the coming of the "Jean Marchand Dam"?
I do not know if that dam has been built yet or not. I just point to these regional pressures that exert themselves in politics. We are all human. I suspect that if the government stays in power those same regional pressures will exert themselves with respect to the application of this bill.
What does the bill really do? Basically, it does three things. It gives the power to block or curtail new foreign money coming into Canada. It gives the power to limit the change of direction of foreign investment already in Canada. For example, I suppose Imperial Oil of Canada would be able to continue to operate in the oil industry here but would not get approval to go into any other line of business. Worst of all, the bill has the power to direct investment within Canada. Perhaps my suspicious mind is at work, but I think it might be said that if this agency is to deal with regional situations an application might be made to start a new factory in Alberta with German or Japanese or any foreign money and the agency might just say "Sorry, we cannot allow any more foreign investment in Alberta. It has too much already and we think it will significantly harm Canada, but you can invest it in some other area." That is where the regional pressures may be exerted.
I think the amendment offered by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), which states that a majority of the panel hearing the application must come from the region to which the application is applied is a sound one. I remember when DREE was established the minister told this House in good faith that he knew of the political pressures and of all the porkbarrelling accusations that could be made, but he said he would try his best to administer the act in a non-partisan way for the good of the country. He tried his best and as Walter Stewart has said, he was able to publish a colourful brochure listing the $270 million in federal grants that had been pumped into his own area since 1967. So, I do not believe his best is good enough, but it was human. I believe that the agency to be set up by this bill would be just as human and as subject to as many pressures. That is why I think the amendment should be supported.
Another area of the bill which gives me concern is the section containing the words "significant benefit to a part
Foreign Investment Review Act of Canada". What particular part, Mr. Speaker? In other words, if the agency questions an application, the applicant must prove that his investment is likely to create significant benefits for Canada. It might well be said that Michelin was a tremendous benefit to the province of Nova Scotia, but it could be argued, too, by another region of Canada that it destroyed the Dunlop Tire Company in the city of Toronto. The words "significant to the benefit of Canada" are not good enough unless there is some regional representation when hearing the application. The wording would make some sense then. There is no doubt in my mind that Michelin would be of significant benefit to the province of Nova Scotia, but they must know that they have to compete with the other industries in Canada. If they want to move into the markets in central Canada, they know that they have to compete. I believe that term denotes that the part of Canada affected will be all right if it has political clout. If it does not have political clout, however, it will have to go begging and it may be heard or it may not. I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that as a member of parliament I should assist the passage of legislation that forces people to go begging. Some criteria should be established for equal treatment and a fair hearing. As the representative of my constituents I can ask no more, but I do ask that and I am sure it is no more than any other member of the House asks.
I would like to go into the question of cost, Mr. Speaker. We are told that the whole purpose of this bill was to stop the sale of Home Oil to Ashland in the United States. If that is so, why play around with the figure of $250,000? I think Home Oil sold for something in the neighbourhood of $30 million, so if the object was to stop the sale of Home Oil it is not necessary to also stop all the little enterprises that may come into this country. By that I mean little, individual investments.
Back in 1909 many of my constituents came to this country as American or Japanese citizens. Indeed, many Japanese citizens were forced to move from Vancouver to my area during the last war. But if they came from the United States or Japan or Holland or Germany, they all became first class Canadian citizens.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: They made an investment here. I think the purpose of the foreign investment bill should be to give a board or an agency the right to examine large corporate investments in Canada, not individual investments. A lot of good automotive agencies would not be sold for less than $250,000. There are even a few farms in some of the choice areas of Alberta that could not be bought for $250,000. In my own area, where it is pretty dry, one might be able to get a toe hold for less than that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: I do not think so.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
The hon. member says he does not think so. Let us suppose for a moment that he is right Who are we saving the land for, and if it is the sale of land that we are trying to block, are we not being unconstitu tional? The hon. member shakes his head in a negative manner. I say that the federal government has no right to interfere with the sale of property within a province. Property belongs to the province. In no way would this

November 6, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act government interfere with the sale of property within the province of Quebec. Let us not fool ourselves about that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: It says "business enterprise".

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, I keep telling my sons that the ranch I am attempting to run is a business enterprise. I sometimes refer to it as a blotter because it soaks up all the money I make. In any case, it is a business enterprise and many farms are business enterprises. If the bill excludes agricultural lands, then the minister should introduce an amendment to this effect or should say that this bill will not interfere with agricultural land in any way, shape or form. The minister steadfastly examines his papers and does not indicate yea or nay to that because he does not want to reach that conclusion. The minister wants this agency to have the power available if it wishes to use it.
I do not believe in the attitude of the province of Saskatchewan with regard to land, Mr. Speaker. I think it is a curse on the agriculture industry of that province. The idea that the government should be the only purchaser and that all lands would revert to the province means that the farmers and ranchers will become like the serfs of the feudal days-they will be serving the government master; the buildings will decay and the land will become non-productive. I do not believe in that. If the minister is headed in that direction, I think we should be told about it before the bill is passed. If he is, he has bought the NDP's concept of socialism, hook, line and sinker. I would not believe it of him, but we certainly have not been told otherwise.
I read the speech of the hon. member for Yorkton-Mel-ville (Mr. Nystrom). He said that his party was not all that fussy about this bill, as it is not strong enough. He went on to say that the screening agency ought to be more powerful, but as the legislation did not say that it had to be more powerful, he rejected the legislation.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: That's the point.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Yes, that is the point. Now, you can see why so many people have been moving out of Saskatchewan and into Alberta. When I go back to my homeland, I am very disheartened. I see the potential there; but developing it takes capital. Considering the attitude of the government of the province, raising such capital will be difficult.
If this agency is set up, will it be instrumental in blocking deals such as the sale of Home Oil to Ashland in the United States? Or, would it block, for instance, the sale of Denison Mines to interests of the Hudson's Bay Company in the United States. Must it play around with every deal that is worth over $200,000?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Sure it must.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: An hon. member to my left says, "Sure it must."

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: What about Saskatchewan?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Let me tell hon. members that Saskatchewan contains more mineral wealth than Alberta.

We do not have as much petroleum wealth but, certainly, we have more mineral wealth. You will not find copper, potash or uranium in Alberta. Those metals are not there, but they are in Saskatchewan. The province has great potential wealth, yet remains on the list of "have-not" areas of this country. Why? Because governments have not encouraged Canadians to invest a nickel in the development of that area. Actually, Canadians leave Saskatchewan and come to Alberta if they want to invest any money, because they enjoy living in the freer atmosphere of that province.
For the reasons I have outlined, I ask the House to accept the amendment standing in my name, which has been put forward in good faith and which asks the amount of $250,000 as provided for in the bill, be changed to $500,000. Surely, if inflation continues at present rates, $500,000 will not be worth much in a few years.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: It will be enough to buy a garden.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Soon, that will be the price of a house.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
One hon. member suggests that soon that amount will just about buy a garden and another hon. member suggests that it will only buy a house. According to some predictions, by the year 2000 a house in Toronto will cost $250,000, if present inflation rates continue. For that reason I submit that the amendment standing in my name ought to be accepted.
As well, the minister ought to consider a number of suggestions contained in the five motions to amend the bill which the House is now considering. The bill could operate very successfully for the whole of Canada if it took into account regional needs. As well as considering the amount of money which might be involved in any transaction, the government should say that the bill will not apply to agricultural property. I suppose the government will say that only businesses are to be affected. I suppose some members of the government think that the family farm is not a business. Well, if they do not consider it as a business, not many farms will survive under the present Liberal administration.
A financier went on television in Toronto and said that Canadians have all kinds of money to invest in Canada. Well, Torontonians have not been too generous in investing money north of Highway 401. They have not been too generous with northern Ontario, with the area west of the Lakehead in Ontario or, for that matter, with any area outside the province of Ontario. So, that financier, that Torontonian, who suggested that the people of Toronto and of Canada have lots of money to invest in this country, perhaps is thinking as the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville is thinking. That hon. member suggested that Canadians have lots of money for the development of Canada. That being so, how is it that so much money is leaving Canada? Too much Canadian money is being invested elsewhere. I see the hon. member nodding affirmatively. I would not wish to misrepresent his position. Why is so much money leaving Canada?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
It is foreign owned.
November 6, 1973

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
If we tax Canadian companies more heavily than we tax internationally set up companies, will we not encourage Canadians to invest in international companies, or in internationally set up companies which operate in Canada? Look at the food industries; very few are not internationally set up. Why? They were forced into that arrangement because of our tax measures. Are they better able to operate that way?
Consider our farm machinery companies. Massey-Fer-gusson, once a Canadian firm, is now an international firm. A whole host of companies which started out as Canadian companies have now become international companies. During the last seven or eight years Massey-Fer-gusson periodically threatened to move its plants entirely out of Canada, down to Detroit. Why? The company blamed the tax laws of Canada. Last spring the company threatened to move its combine plant from Brantford, Ontario, to Detroit. Why? The reason, again has to do with the tax laws of Canada.
In considering foreign investment within Canada, we must not forget that we must also encourage Canadians to invest in Canada. Consider, as well, what has happened to the oil industry. What has happened in the past will continue to happen under the tyranny of the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald). He is not interested so much in the long-term well being of Canada, and the encouragement of investment in the oil industry, as in dominating that significant industry.
Many have commented about wealthy Alberta and about how Alberta sold out its oil resources to the extent that it is now almost wholly foreign controlled. Alberta did not sell out. The federal government in Ottawa forced the Canadian-owned oil industry to leave the province. Why was Home Oil forced to sell out to Consumers Gas of Toronto. What were the considerations respecting the Ashland deal? I submit that the oil company was forced to sell out because of the operation of our Canadian tax laws. It had undertaken exploration for oil around the world and in Canada, and was in financial trouble. The company was badly in the hole. It was necessary to find a buyer who would bail the company out of its deficit position. If our tax laws had been adjusted, it would not have been in that deficit position. If our tax laws had not been designed to be of benefit, as they are, to international oil companies, it is possible that Home Oil would not have been forced to seek a buyer. Putting it simply, moral suasion on the part of the government-I say that because the government had not legal power in the matter-forced Home Oil to sell out to Consumers Gas of Toronto, that company being preferred to an American oil company.
One could argue, of course, as I have heard people from western Canada and other regions argue, that the profits of the Home Oil operation will be reaped in Toronto. They will not be readily reinvested in the oil industry, but will be reinvested in the construction industry of Toronto and southern Ontario. One could argue that if Home Oil had been sold to Ashland of Canada, Ashland of Canada would have ploughed some of its profits back into the oil industry of Alberta. Perhaps we might not be as short of oil as we are today. I do not know. It seems to me that there may be some merit in giving the government some power to
Foreign Investment Review Act control the sales of corporations. Earlier today someone mentioned Canadian General Electric, General Motors, Ford and the other big automotive manufacturers. Maybe we could include Home Oil and Denison Mines. Perhaps the government does need an agency to screen foreign take-overs of large concerns like that.
There are all kinds of small towns in my constituency that would love to have some investment in industry. I have put a few thousand dollars into small industries in my constituency over the past 25 years. I lost money on two of them. Invariably, the trouble was getting finances to cover the value of inventory the industry built up and was not able to sell readily. If the products could have been sold as fast as they were made, the company would have stayed in business. Anyone who knows anything about industry knows it is necessary to build up an inventory. If you make a product that sells in the summer, you must build up an inventory of that product in the winter. The value of inventory will eventually kill a small corporation if it does not receive some capital. The industries in the town to which I am referring went begging to the United States to try to get a little foreign investment. They were not able to and, as a result, the two companies went broke.
I have another concern. Recently one of the biggest industries in my constituency was purchased with Japanese money. The owner went hither and yon looking for Canadian money. He spent months in Toronto and Montreal. He visited the head offices of every major chartered bank in Canada. He came away with a sad reflection. I find it sad because it is becoming a more and more accepted reflection in Canada. The owner told me he was going to sell the controlling interest in his plant to the Japanese. I said that was bad. He told me that, in addition to spending months in Toronto and Montreal, he had received a DREE grant. It took a year or two, but he finally got the money. He had reached the conclusion that eastern Canada was not interested in western Canada. I found that terribly sad. I am not referring to the oil industry, but to what might be called an industrial side of the agricultural complex. He said he had to go to Japan to get the money because eastern Canada was not interested in the west.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: That is not true.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Thank you very much. I would rather have heard that from the minister, but I appreciate hearing it from my friend and former colleague, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle). In any event, that is a widely held belief in western Canada today. I think it is a shame. That is why I urge the minister to accept the concept of some kind of regional representation on the panel hearing the application.
I read the briefs that came before the committee. The province of Saskatchewan, because of the NDP philosophy which originates in Toronto with the major unions, does whatever the NDP here wants them to do. That is obvious from their stand on the oil question and on this particular piece of legislation. When representatives of the province of Saskatchewan appeared before the committee, what did

November 6, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act they say? They said that this legislation needs a little more provincial input. They said they completely buy the concept of some agency controlling foreign investment, but would like to have a little more regional or provincial input. What did the premier of New Brunswick say? Speaking for the four Atlantic provinces, he said they, too, want some consideration.
This bill will probably pass, maybe tonight; I do not know. However, if it does pass, in spite of the extremities of Canada complaining and asking for a little regional representation, if the minister rides roughshod over them, he is not doing Canada a service. He is being arrogant, like the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), and is not paying attention. We are a confederation of regions, a federation of provinces. A few years ago in this House the common expression among all parties was federal co-operative.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Co-operative federalism.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: That is another way of saying exactly what I said. I am pleased to hear the hon. member express it. I wish he were a member of the cabinet. I wish some minister would use that expression every other day or at least once a week. It would be very pleasing to the regions of Canada that do not have a political clout if they could get a little more attention.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Does Lougheed believe in that?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
The premier of Alberta has said time and again that Canada will not go short of oil if he has anything to do about it. He said Canada will not have to pay a price higher than the world price for oil. He said that Canadians will not necessarily have to pay what Americans will have to pay as a result of their foreign policy. Alberta wants fair and equal treatment with regard to its resources, just as New Brunswick wants for its resources and as Toronto wants for its resources and, I might say, has received.
The oil companies have no control over oil in the province of Alberta. The Alberta government controls the oil. It determines how much comes out of the ground, who takes it out and where it goes, whether it crosses provincial boundaries or stays within Alberta. That is the sole prerogative of the Alberta government. That is a jpoint that must be considered when talking about the oil industry.
While speaking about the oil industry, I wonder what political clout the 17 per cent of the Canadian people had who voted for the party on my left and socialism.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: 20 per cent.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: I think it was 17.8 per cent, if my memory is correct. I did not look at the hon. member's figures. He can examine mine. Only 17.8 per cent voted for socialism, yet we are getting it in great gobs.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Not enough.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
After reading the speech of the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville, I wondered how much money he has ever tried to raise. I wondered how much money he has invested in some of the small companies

around Yorkton. I do not know whether or not he has graduated from university. The last time I asked him, he was still going.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: He pays his taxes.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: He pays his taxes.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Yes, and you give them away.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
I don't. Le us look at the Syncrude project. Let us look at the tar sands. The tar sands of northern Alberta were known 200 years ago, around 1775. The first government study of those tar sands was done in 1875. We are now getting close to 1975, and we are barely getting some of the oil out. The Premier of Alberta has gone to great lengths to encourage the development of this resource. Time and time again he has said the only thing which will bring the Arabs to the negotiating table in a proper frame of mind with regard to the price of oil is the presence of alternative oil resources. Well, there are 15,000 square miles of tar sands in northern Alberta.
The Syncrude project, which involves four oil companies, is to cover eight square miles. It will take them 25 years to complete their operations in this area, and to this end it will be necessary for them to raise $1,200 million in capital. We need another company alongside Syncrude. But taking into account the frame of, mind of the present government, dominated as it is by that small block to my left, people who say they want socialism up there to develop the tar sands-

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Right on!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Order. I regret having to interrupt the hon. member but the time allotted to him has expired.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Continue.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Might I continue?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: That can only be done by unanimous consent. Does the House agree?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Thank you. I appreciate the generosity of the House.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Socialist generosity.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
I have learned over the years that the only thing socialists are generous with is their time. They like to talk. They are very poor at producing anything, but they certainly like to talk. And it seems that at times they do not mind listening.
I was referring to the gigantic size of the tar sands- 15,000 square miles-and the huge capital investment needed to develop a mere eight square miles in 25 years. In developing this eight square miles, the companies hope to produce 125,000 barrels a day. Now, the Montreal market alone needs 500,000 barrels a day, so if we want to become self-sufficient in Canada more Canadian production is needed. Geologists who have studied the tar sands suggest
November 6, 1973

there- is enough oil there to supply Canada's needs for some 600 years. Production is only now getting started. In the absence of regional representation on the panel hearing an application, and allowing for the frame of mind of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), following the socialists and adhering to the socialist concept which they advance, I can easily envisage a confrontation taking place in the years ahead.
The premier of Alberta might go to Japan and say to businessmen there: We want another Syncrude development, another project. We will give you a lease on a further eight square miles. Come over with your millions; don't go into Siberia and develop oil for the Russians there, but help us develop our oil in the tar sands. This may well be the line taken. Of course, I do not know whether or not he is thinking along those lines. I am suggesting one situation which may be created by this agency. In the absence of regional representation on the board, the answer to the applicant might be "No", and then the Arabs would have things all their own way for another ten years when it comes to the pricing of world crude. The only thing that will bring the Arabs to the negotiating table in a sensible frame of mind with regard to the price of crude oil is the development of an alternate source of supply. If the co-operation of the federal government is forthcoming, the Province of Alberta has the ability to develop such a source. It is sad to reflect that we have not received such co-operation to date. However, we in Alberta believe in the future. We hope and believe that the Lord will hear, and that Macdonald will hear along with him. We hope, too, that other cabinet ministers will be a little more attentive, and a little more appreciative of regional considerations.
I shall end on this note. The government would be doing a terrible disservice to unity, a terrible disservice to cooperative federalism if it refused to pay heed to the wishes of the provinces on the eastern and western extremities of Canada. In western Canada, the government of Saskatchewan, in spite of the dominance exercised by people to my left, has asked that provision be made for more provincial input. The premiers of the four Atlantic Provinces have asked for regional consideration. The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) has placed an amendment before the House, and I ask all hon. members to give it most careful consideration. There is nothing in it which the government could find offensive. If the minister cannot accept the word "majority" let him put in the word "equal". Let him endorse the concept that the provinces have a view to express, and allow them a means of expressing it.
I shall deal briefly with another part of the amendment, which asks that as soon as an application is made it shall be the duty of the minister who speaks for the agency to notify forthwith the region or the province in which the applicant wishes to invest. This is only sensible. This is only courteous. But we know it has not happened under DREE. All kinds of industries have made application to DREE. Sometimes they have been told: Yes, we can give you so much money, but we are really not anxious to see it invested over there, because the unemployment rate is not high enough; if you invest it somewhere else, we can give you a little more. Pressure, as between regions and provinces, has been exerted under DREE. Under one of the
Foreign Investment Review Act amendments we are debating, the provinces concerned would be notified right away and would know what was happening. Provinces would know when a company was likely to leave their jurisdiction. They might say, as the people of Saskatchewan would say: "Good riddance". But they might, on the other hand, say, as Albertans would say: "Stick here with your investment".
I propose to end by returning to the subject of my own amendment, as seems only reasonable. I know that a large number of companies began with an investment of less than $200,000. Take the Claresholm Airport as an example. Little companies got started, with the help of United States money in two instances, and today the operation is completely owned by Canadians. There was no harm in these small companies getting started in this way. One of them, a huge company now, is completely owned by Canadians. This is an example of an enterprise capable of being started in a small way. I do not think the agency should concern itself with anything less than a million dollars. But I was modest when framing my amendment because I like the government to accept my ideas-and the government has accepted a good many of them. This government has accepted many of my ideas, but the minister has not accepted one. I should like him to accept the proposition that the sum of $250,000, with the terrible inflation that his colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has allowed to arise in Canada, is not a large amount and that it should be increased to at least $500,000.
Having abused the House with this lengthy speech, the House having been generous in allowing me to speak at length, I might advise hon. members that I shall speak again on the other set of amendments.
