subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words on Bill C-132.
A lot has been written and a lot has been said in recent days on Parliament Hill about this bill. We have all known for quite some time, Mr. Speaker, that we are faced with great problems and those problems are complex.
We know also, Mr. Speaker, that there are ways of solving those problems, particularly in respect of foreign exports, foreign takeovers of our industries and natural resources.
If foreigners own 50 per cent or perhaps 80 per cent of industries and businesses in Canada they are not to blame; we should censure those Canadian leaders who failed to foresee it, who failed to pass the needed regulations and who failed to adjust the economy to facts and reality so all Canadians could own their own, and own and develop their natural resources.
Our resources, Mr. Speaker, are developed by foreigners and we must ask ourselves why. Do we lack technology in Canada? Do we lack labour?
If we do not lack technology, if we do not lack labour, what do we lack, Mr. Speaker? Surely if we lack technology we could import it. That is what one could call foreign capital. After using that technology and acquiring the required knowledge for the developments we want to bring about, then it would be up to us Canadians to either continue using it, keep it or reject it.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot even develop our technology without financing and if foreigners now own the major part of our resources, our developments, our industries, it is because they made the necessary capital available to those who wanted to develop them.
Here in Canada there was a failure to understand what capital is; there was a lack of readiness to use the organizations available that could create the required capital for developments we have to bring into being.
Foreigners availed themselves of that right and created capital on those same assets, those assets we owned, those assets to be developed. They created capital as the developments became possible. That is what we failed to do.
This is what even now few members tell the House; in this way they would find the mean to develop our natural resources and help our future industries. Mr. Speaker, the
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel).]
government has devised a system to promote industrial development.
We find, Mr. Speaker, that a large number of industries are going bankrupt, in spite of the help they received from governments. Then, where is the problem? Capital is placed at the disposal of industries but they cannot operate; it only extends their lives by a few years and eventually they go under. Why? Because the means placed at the disposal of industries by governments are only a restraint, a way to deprive them even more.
Mr. Speaker, a small enterprise has to go deeper into debt in order to benefit from the advantages placed at its disposal. All members know that: a company that wants to receive a $20,000 government subsidy must invest itself $100,000 which amount it does not have because it has been overtaxed in every possible way by governments. The company does not have the capital required for the developments it would like to achieve. Then the Industrial Development Bank was created to loan money to businesses. In order to grant them a $20,000 subsidy we loan $100,000 at the present usurious interest rate of 10 or 12 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, this is not logical. This is taking an unfair advantage because interest rates are too high. So, a small manufacturer who owes $100,000, $200,000 or $1 million, according to the importance of his business, has to repay enormous amounts which are taxed at 40, 50 and even 60 per cent. The small manufacturers cannot afford those exhorbitant interest rates and the enormous taxes they have to pay. This is why nothing can be developped. Almost everything we try to develop is a failure. Such operation gives rise to the accumulation of enormous debts and those who succeed have to work perhaps 10 to 15 hours a day and through hard work they make profits, they increase prices. A few sometimes succeed in this system but at the expense of others. If one succeeds, it is because others have failed. Indeed, they are prevented from succeeding.
Mr. Speaker, we are seeking solutions to that problem. We blame foreigners because they invest here and control our resources. Now I am convinced that we will never regain the ownership of our resources and our institutions if we do not alter our financing procedure which is outmoded, obsolete and leads any industry or enterprise to ruin.
As long as we won't come to grips with this evil, we will get the same results. And the further we go, even if we pass legislation and regulations to side-step foreign investments, or if we tax part of these investments, the more we will paralyze the economy, the greater will be our disappointments. We will experience an increase in the level of unemployment, privations and strikes. But, where can we find a solution? Solutions are right there at hand. If we want to launch a new enterprise in a logical fashion, it will have to be financed through new credits free of interest. We could launch new enterprises in this manner. We will never achieve anything in a 100 years if we continue to pile up debts, otherwise we will continue to keep Canadians under the yoke, to increase taxes and the number of civil servants, thus bringing about an increase in the cost of living, as it happens at present.
November 6, 1973

Where are we going with all these gimmicks, all these outmoded wild dreams, Mr. Speaker? Where does it all lead us to? It leads us directly to ruin. We are on the brinkmanship of bankruptcy, we are nearing a revolution.
Mr. Speaker, if foreigners can find capital by coining money, we can do the same. If the United States find that developments are inadequate and they require them, and if these developments are obvious and profitable, they will create new capital and thus enable industry to operate. They will allow access to capital at a much more reasonable interest rate than that charged by the Industrial Development Bank which exploits industries to the extreme.
Mr. Speaker, we must think about this and stop moaning and blaming foreigners. We must confess our own sins because we are the ones who have jeopardized our own development. If development is not progressing as it should, again we are the culprits, not foreigners.
In fact, foreigners cannot benefit from the resources made available by our financial institutions. We are the ones who, within our government, can ask our organizations to issue such or such credit at a small rate of interest or at none whatsoever. No foreigners will come here to do it for us. And failing to do it, we will go on having the disappointments we are now suffering and realizing that we are no longer our masters at home, that everything belongs to foreigners. And if this is so, Mr. Speaker, it would be time to find a solution to such a problem.
This bill will not solve the problem. In spite of our intentions to restrict foreign investments, will we find Canadian capital to fill the gap?
Those are the problems the bill should solve, but it offers no serious remedy. According to the bill, some foreign investments must be controlled and reported. But how will it help the provinces in developing our country?
If there were fewer taxes, if we had a balanced economy, in accordance with facts, Canadians would have more purchasing power and make the industry work appropriately. It would not even need the Industrial Development Bank, nor the chartered banks.
If industry could sell its products to Canadians, we would not need all the agencies we have now. Industries could develop if governments would not saddle them with taxes, if they were not saddled with them all. We are driving all businesses and all industries into bankruptcy because of taxes, heavy taxes, and we will let the taxpayers pay for everything.
We are told that private industry has gone bankrupt. No wonder since it is cut off at source. If we do everything to keep people from getting what they want, it is hard for them to do anything.
We are building all sorts of barriers to stop the Canadians who would like to go further and do something. We shut them in and use all possible means to prevent them from going ahead. We find it sad that all our capital and institutions are in foreign hands.
Once again, we are to blame, Mr. Speaker, and we shall never be able to develop our country, our resources and our institutions if the required capital is not made avail-
Foreign Investment Review Act able to Canadians at reasonable interest rates and if we do not lower taxes. There is no other way that we can own something in Canada. We are now losing more and more ground, businesses and industries, and we are becoming less and less able to develop our natural resources because we do not have the required capital. The government is not trying to make this capital available to Canadian citizens. This is why we are in the hands of foreigners; the situation will worsen until they have a large enough share of Canadian business to take over the entire country. That time is perhaps not too far away.

speechtext:
I think that perhaps Progressive Conservative members opposite have not yet understood or recognized the importance of that point.
The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) referred to regional pressures. He seemed to be suggesting that somehow or other the minister would reflect, whoever that minister might be at any particular time, his own perspective. I should like to assure him and all hon. members opposite that the process of the allowance or disallowance of a proposed takeover or the establishment of a new business is clearly laid out; that the minister will be advised by the officials in the foreign investment review agency, that he will make recommendations, and that the cabinet will decide. So, clearly, if there is concern that the regional interests of Canada will not be reflected at the decision-making point, I hope the hon. member will recognize that the cabinet is the ultimate decision-making body which reflects the regional interests of this great nation.
There was one other point that the hon. member for Crowfoot made. As I listened to him, he seemed to suggest that this bill would in some way provide the government, through the foreign investment review agency, with an instrument for directing investment within Canada. He suggested that this would be a bad thing. Let me assure him that this is simply not true, that the bill itself does not provide, nor does it give to the minister the power to direct investment within Canada. It gives the minister the power to recommend the allowance or disallowance of an investment. It gives the minister and the government the power to bargain for benefits if those benefits are not present in the proposal itself.
Mr. Speaker, I would like now to deal specifically with each of the three amending motions dealing in particular with the question of the provincial interest. I will start with motion No. 2. On first reading it sounds plausible because it restates, or appears to restate, the particular clause I quoted a moment ago, clause 2 (2) (e), with respect to the criterion of significant benefit to Canada. It appears to divide that clause into two paragraphs; in fact,
November 6, 1973

one has to look rather more carefully at it because it does more than that.
It is not just a question of form. It is very certainly an amendment with respect to substance, because this particular amendment talks about "the compatability of the acquisition or establishment with industrial and economic policies enunciated by the government or legislature of a province in which the enterprise is carried on or the new business is proposed to be carried on." That is new language; it is different language from that which appears in the bill itself. The bill now provides for the government to take into account "industrial and economic policy objectives ... of any province likely to be significantly affected by the acquisition or establishment."
The amendment focuses only on the province in which the enterprise is carried on or in which the new business is proposed to be carried on. Secondly, the amendment would make it appear that provincial industrial and economic policies would have slightly higher priority than they are accorded in the current bill. I would point out that in the current bill provincial policies are referred to in the same paragraph as national policies. In the amendment they are referred to in a separate paragraph, but the distinction here is not great.
In speaking to this proposed amendment, the following points might be made: by abandoning the words "by . .. any province likely to be significantly affected" the amendment can have a perverse effect in two distinct ways. Let us suppose a firm to be acquired has five plants, in five separate provinces in Canada, but has a substantial plant in only one of them and very small ones in the other four. The amendment would not, on the face of it, give government the authority to attach relatively greater weight to the policy of the province in which the large plant is located.
Conversely, it is quite conceivable that a province may be affected in a very substantial way by a takeover or a new investment, even if the firm to be acquired or the investment which is to be made is not within that province. The province may have a very large interest in a takeover or investment because of its position as a consuming province or because there are plants in the province which are competitive with the firm to be taken over or established. Thus, doing away with the words "by . .. any province likely to be significantly affected" is a step backward. It would remove an essential flexibility from the bill, and that would have the effect of seriously undercutting its effectiveness.
I would now like to turn to motions Nos. 5 and 6. Motion No. 5, also in this general area of provincial or regional interests, was moved by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). I would like to read it in order to put it in context. It is to delete subclause 7(3), lines 23 to 28, page 18, and substitute therefor the following:
The minister shall make available to the agency the services of officers who are representative of each region of Canada, including such officers from within the department of the Government of Canada over which he presides as he may designate for the purpose.
In any case where a review or assessment of a proposed or actual investment is likely to affect significantly a province or provinces, a recommendation to the minister thereon shall be
Foreign Investment Review Act
submitted by a panel of officers of whom a majority shall be representative of such province or provinces.
The proposal has two parts. The first is that the minister should supply the agency with the services of officers who are "representative of each region of Canada". This may include officers from within his own department. Secondly, whenever the agency makes a recommendation to the minister concerning a foreign investment, the recommendation shall be made "by a panel of officers of whom a majority shall be representative of such province or provinces" likely to be significantly affected.
The proposed amendment can be criticized from two points of view. It is technically weak, and the policy implications conflict with the intention of the bill. Let me deal first with the technical points. It is not clear what is meant by "region." This is a new concept. It does not enter into the bill, nor is it defined anywhere in the bill itself. So one wonders whether the drafter intended "region" or "province." It is not clear. Nor is it clear what a "representative" would be. This is clearly a new concept not to be found elsewhere in the bill. And the drafter does not suggest any definition of the term "representative" because neither "region" nor "representative" are defined. Similarly, it is not clear what would constitute a "panel of officers." In any event, a federal agency cannot be administered by "representatives" of provinces or regions. This, I suggest, is a naive concept when considered carefully. It can only be administered by people who are unequivocally employed by the federal government.
This is to be an act of parliament. The governor in council is responsible for the decisions, not some ill-defined group of officers who are employees, who are there to analyse and advise but not to decide. Those are technical points. Now I would like to deal with the policy points. The implication of the proposed amendment is that the legislation should be administered in a way which would reflect regional views almost exclusively. Such a view conflicts with a central purpose of the bill, which is to establish and apply a national foreign investment policy. When provinces compete to attract the investor, this has the effect of reducing the benefits which are potentially available to Canada and to the provinces.
Secondly, the interests of the provinces are already well protected. I have reference to the inclusion of two other areas in the bill, one dealing with the transference of information which provides the essential authority for forwarding information to the provinces. But, Mr. Speaker, we must surely avoid amendments which would bal-kanize the bill. Provincial interests are safeguarded by several provisions, particularly the requirement to take into account stated provincial policies in clause 2(2)(e), page 2; the requirement for the minister to take into account provincial representations in clause 9(d), page 21; and the fact that the minister has explicit authority in clause 14(2) (b), page 26, to make available to a minister or official of a provincial government information relating to a proposed takeover or new investment which has been submitted by the potential investor.
It cannot be stressed too often that the bill will not block foreign investment which is needed by any particu-

November 6, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act lar region. The purpose of the bill is to improve the net benefit to Canada, and the provisions of the bill will provide the government with the authority to negotiate with investors to obtain increased benefits for Canadians. For these reasons I would reject the amendment on both technical and policy grounds.
Let me turn to the other two amendments in this general area proposed by the hon. member for Central Nova. In one, amendment No. 6, he moves that clause 9 be amended by deleting line 32, at page 20, and substituting the following:
"a copy of the notice shall be sent by the agency forthwith by registered mail to the province or provinces likely to be significantly affected by the proposed or actual investment to which the notice relates and"
Mr. Speaker, the effect of accepting this amendment would be to quite drastically change the administration of this bill. I recall that the hon. member said he was concerned about the bureaucratic process involved in administering the bill. I am concerned about it too, Mr. Speaker, because it is a technical and sensitive area. However, the effect of this particular amendment would be to increase enormously the degree of bureaucratic input. It would require the agency to provide all the information with respect to any proposed transaction, and all the information with respect to any takeover or establishment of any new business in all provinces. I think it would be helpful if I were to indicate why I think that might happen. Under the bill, notice under clause 8(1), 8(2) or 8(3) is provided for as follows:
. . . notice in writing to the agency of such proposal in such form and manner and containing such information as is prescribed by the regulations.
It is not simply an indication in writing that a takeover or an investment has taken place. It is, in effect, all the information which the applicant provides. The amendment proposes that the notice and all the information which is part of it, much of which will be confidential to the business, be sent not only to the proposed province of location but it makes mandatory that it be sent to all provinces which are likely to be significantly affected. This could involve virtually all provinces; it would not be clear who would determine whether a province was significantly affected or not. For example, a new tire plant might be considered for an area of the Maritimes. The argument might be that the only other province to be affected would be Nova Scotia-if we think of the Miche-lin situation-but clearly several provinces might be significantly benefited or affected by such an investment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we recessed for the dinner hour we had been dealing with a set of amendments. Three motions, in particular Nos. 2, 5 and 6, deal with an area of provincial or regional concern, although the purport of those amendments is not altogether clear.
I said that after the dinner-hour recess I would be dealing with the other set of amendments which have to do with thresholds with respect to the takeover of Canadian companies. In this regard we should consider two amendments, one of which has been brought forward by the hon. member for Crowfoot, and the other by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). They show that there is not any one magic figure which ought to apply to thresholds; that is to say, there is no magic figure at which the screening process should become operative.
On the one hand, the hon. member for Crowfoot feels that the thresholds in the bill are too low and should be raised. His amendment suggests that the threshold concerning the gross assets of a corporation should be raised from $250,000 to $500,000. On the other hand, the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville feels that perhaps thresholds are too high and should be lowered. He suggests that in view of the second test-and there are two with respect to thresholds, one having to do with gross assets and the other with respect to revenues and sales-the figure should be lowered.
The hon. member for Crowfoot says that we should raise the threshold, that we should double the amount of assets which must be considered in connection with the threshold. The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville says that we should cut in half the threshold which applies to revenues and sales and in that regard we should reduce it from $3 million to $1.5 million.
The issue we face is clearly this: Is there any right figure? I suggest to hon. members that the threshold, by its very nature, represents an arbitrary figure. It will never satisfy everybody. It will never satisfy all interests. However, we hope that it can be a practical working figure which will satisfy the great bulk of Canadian opinion. On the one hand there is an amendment suggesting that we should raise one of the tests, that we should double the figure, and on the other hand there is an amendment suggesting that we should cut one of the tests in half. The
November 6, 1973

bill clearly stakes out the middle ground which is acceptable to most Canadians.
The hon. member for Crowfoot felt that the threshold was too low, that perhaps too many smaller corporations might be considered under it. He felt that those smaller corporations, in the very nature of things, might not be important. I suggest to him that one of the important aspects of this bill is that it concerns itself with the "comers", the growth industries, the high-technology industries and those small companies that are of concern to the cultural development of Canada. Clearly, if we were to raise to $500,000 the threshold with respect to gross assets, we would remove from the screening process a large number of firms. In my view, and in the government's view, that would not be in the Canadian public interest.
Too often in our history Canadians have developed new and important technology only to find that it slips from our grasp and that other countries obtain the commercial advantages which flow from it. The amendment of the hon. member for Crowfoot is, in my view, such an invitation; it will allow more of this technology to slide across the border-

It is important from the point of view of the operation of the bill; that is to say, it will assist those who are concerned with the administration of this legislation to administer the test in a sensible and operative way.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-132 sets up a mechanism for the control and operation of foreign investment in Canada. We are entering a new phase and a new direction in our investment policy. I hope the minister will see fit to increase the input of the provinces to this investment tribunal. This is the only way there can be some input from the periphery of the country. In his attempt to throw out the amendments, the minister stated that provincial input is not needed, that this is only a tribunal of investment people and bureaucrats who will make recommendations to cabinet, which in turn will decide fairly and honestly whether the investments should be permitted.
The present experience with the Wheat Board is a good example. The Wheat Board is acting contrary to the interests of many provinces. The pricing of feed grains is considerably less per bushel for barley, wheat and oats than on the markets of the world. In other words, instead of an export tax on oil to the United States, the Wheat Board has instituted a selling policy that is a discounting of grain to feeders and a subsidy to the consumer. If the government wants to subsidize the consumer, this should be done in some other way.
I remind the minister that the Manitoba minister of Agriculture is prepared to seek an injunction in the Court of Queen's Bench because the Wheat Board is not selling grain at the maximum price. A feature story in the Gazette states as follows;
Mr. Uskiw hopes his lawyers will tell him that Manitoba can make a case that the Wheat Board Act instructs the board at all times to sell for a maximum price for the farmer . . .
If Mr. Uskiw cannot make his case stick in Court of Queen's Bench, he may go to the Supreme Court of Canada. On the other hand, if he is given advice not to proceed along these lines at all, he will try another tack that, again, involves constitutional questions covering trade and commerce.
The Canadian Wheat Board was established to pursue a course of action in the interest of the western farmer. I suggest this investment tribunal will be in the same category. After all, the Wheat Board is a selling mechanism for 200,000 permit holders or 800,000 men, women and children. If cabinet can order the Wheat Board to institute policies that are not in the interest of western farmers, they can certainly order any tribunal and direct any investment in a manner that is not conducive to the region affected. I suggest that the Wheat Board would not oper-

November 6, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act ate in the same way if it were dealing with the citizens of Ontario and Quebec because those provinces are large enough to have an effect on the actions of this government body.
Canadians, obviously, have ambivalent feelings about foreign investment. Many people now think it fashionable to regard foreign investment as a bad thing even though by any stretch of the imagination internal Canadian savings would not have been nearly enough to have generated the capital necessary to develop our resources to the stage they are now and give our people the high standard of living that we want and to which we are accustomed. It is fashionable to say that if we had not allowed foreign capital to be invested in our country, we would be better off. I remind those people that the standard of living attained in decades gone by would not have been possible without foreign investment. A classic example is the western oil industry. Until the advent of Leduc in 1954, Canada was totally dependent on offshore and American oil. With the discovery of oil in Alberta, the Canadian industrial capacity markedly increased.
Did Canadian money flow into the development of the western Canadian oil fields? Of course not. What money was available was concentrated in Montreal and Toronto in their own investment needs. They did not invest in western oil. One cannot blame them for that. In fact, most of the drilling for western oil was financed by people south of our border. This was not done by large companies but by individuals, the type of people who like to gamble in high-risk investments. I am referring to those people who like to put in $3,000, $4,000 or $5,000 on an investment. If they lost, fine. If they won, the rewards were big. The American tax department favoured these people for losses incurred anywhere in the world. American taxpayers could deduct this from income. The result was that American individuals contributed a great deal to the finding of oil in western Canada, plus a limited amount as a result of the investment of western Canadian money.
At the present time, most of the drilling by Americans in Alberta is being carried out by independent drillers and is financed in much the same way. We in Canada have followed another tack. In the late forties, many people in western Canada invested in western oil. However, the government changed the tax regulations. The investment could not be deducted unless there was a find. The money dried up immediately. Those who would have contributed to the finding of oil in western Canada were pretty well left out. It took 20 years to have this changed whereby there would be some redress or incentive for those who wanted to invest in this high-risk venture.
It is fashionable to blame our oil prices on American companies. The export tax is justified on the basis that it is only taking from American companies, and that is just and honest. However, without American investment in oil it does not seem likely that the western Canadian industry, even at this stage, would be big enough to supply all of western Canada. Perhaps it should be this way, but it would have added immeasurably to our present problems.
Then again, in the October issue of the Labour Gazette, on page 643, we find a small news item stating that

Oakville, Ontario, was the city with the highest average income of any Canadian city in 1971. The report adds that Oakville is the site of the Ford Motor Company, a company with a substantial component of U.S. investment. Questions which have been raised in this House suggest that the auto pact is showing signs of not working in Canada's favour, and one gathers from a point made by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) that these corporations are not investing enough money in new plant expansion in Canada.
The government of Manitoba made a great effort to entice a Japanese bicycle factory to establish in Rivers, offering it all sorts of grants and encouragement. I draw attention to the fact that this was an NDP government. Incidentally, the new review board which this bill proposes would likely have torpedoed that venture because it would have conflicted with the interests of bicycle manufacturers in the east.
Canadians have complained bitterly about DISC programs adopted by the United States, but DISC was designed to do the very thing this bill would do, that is, to keep American investment at home. The threat of DISC programs was sufficient to cause the government to allow hasty tax concessions to corporations and companies engaged in manufacturing and processing. This gave the central Canadian heartland a great advantage over the peripheral regions where there is little manufacturing and processing. The cut in corporation tax is a foretaste of what is likely to happen under the measure we are now considering; the central heartland of the country will be favoured by this agency to the detriment of the periphery.
Now, Mr. Speaker, foreign investment is necessary only to the extent that Canadians fail to generate enough capital to meet their own needs. There seems to be ample evidence that from the point of view of savings we are generating sufficient capital domestically to meet our requirements, though, of course, there is a good deal of imbalance in the situation. Canadians have obviously quit saving as individuals; they tend to put their money into large pools and there is considerable evidence that they now own a substantial portion of many large Canadian concerns.
The picture has changed considerably in a decade. It may be somewhat doubtful that Canadians will continue to save, since there is much less reason for them to save as individuals than in the past. The effect of old age security legislation, the Canada Pension Plan and the provision of health and welfare care for citizens over 65 means that people can live in reasonable comfort on relatively lower personal savings. The passage of savings from one generation to the next is very effectively discouraged by the capital gains tax and provincial estate taxes. These two taxes combined, especially when the capital gains tax matures, will effectively absorb a good percentage of personal savings. To the self-employed, savings are becoming progressively less valuable even when capital is required as a basis for a working income. So whether or not Canadian savings maintain their present level remains to be seen.
In any case, assuming that Canadian savings are, indeed, sufficient for capital formation requirements, the very size of this country and its regional divisions means
November 6, 1973

that certain areas have access to a high volume of savings, and others to too little. Nor is it easy to move capital from one area to another even if it should be desirable to do so. As our economy matures, I believe we will find it desirable to invest capital around the world, while capital other than Canadian is invested here. Unless we want to build a little Canada with a wall around it, we shall have to follow a policy of this kind. For example, a western Canadian farmer would not, likely, wish to invest in an iron mine in Labrador; but he might well wish to invest in a grain combine, starting his operations in Texas in midsummer and working north right through until the fall, harvesting crops in Canada. This would have obvious advantages as compared with an investment in a project of which he knows nothing and about which he could probably not care less.
The legislation before us has a further flaw inasmuch as it is almost certain to lead to the creation of a czar-like organization of bureaucrats in Ottawa directing the economy of the nation. The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) has pointed out that depending on the attitude of the minister or of the officials, the suggested board could become an extremely severe instrument with monopolistic powers or, alternatively, one which exercised scarcely any authority. My own feeling is that, like the tax department, this body will have a profound effect on Canadian business operations.
Mr. Speaker, there is always a danger attached to an Ottawa-based institution. Like imperial Rome, it tends to regard the distant parts of the country as its own preserve to be saved from the misguided ventures in which those who live out in the periphery will indulge in if left to themselves. Under the new policies, the whole executive level of the federal civil service will be drawn from within the Ottawa Valley and we can expect increasing misunderstanding and disinterest in the affairs of those parts of the country farthest removed from Ottawa.
Equally important, in my view, is the fact that pools of capital are now concentrated in very few hands. Perhaps not more than 50 people are really involved in the investment of these huge sums. The rise in the importance of corporate pension funds, mutual funds, insurance funds and registered retirement funds means that the pools of capital available for investment are very large and very concentrated and that their managers exercise enormous control. A brief presented by the Toronto stock exchange indicated that in 1970 corporate pension funds formed one of the largest pools of investment in Canada, totalling over $10 billion in that year; they ranked only behind life insurance as a pool of capital. Personally, I am concerned lest this grouping of capital in very large pools should in the end work to the detriment of Canadians.
The reason I urge the adoption of these amendments, Mr. Speaker, is that action along the lines they suggest would allow for provincial input into decisions affecting foreign takeover applications. The existence of a bureaucratic group in Ottawa, coupled with the concentration of the investment pools in the financial capitals of Montreal and Toronto, would mean, in effect, that people with little knowledge of conditions in the periphery, and indeed little concern for them, could control investment in those areas removed from the centre.
Foreign Investment Review Act
Many of the situations with which the proposed board would be dealing are likely to concern small Canadian companies, perhaps family-owned, faced with succession duties and the imposition of capital gains taxes. Others will involve rundown plants for which a Canadian buyer cannot be found. I do not see that the foreign investment tribunal will affect the provinces of Quebec and Ontario one iota. The tribunal is not likely to act against the interests of either of these provinces because they are too big and too powerful in their own right. But it would certainly be open season as far as the provinces in the west and in the Maritimes are concerned.
Indeed, the federal government has already declared war on the province of Alberta and is carrying on a feud with Manitoba and Saskatchewan in connection with feed grains and wheat. And it could easily become involved in the B.C. lumber question. The amendments go some way toward encouraging citizens who live in western Canada and in the Maritimes to feel that their views will have some effect on the action of the tribunal.
We might also remember that in the western provinces and the Maritimes are situated a great many of the resources whose development and ownership have aroused more controversy than has arisen in connection with developments elsewhere. Indeed, some Canadians seem to be of the opinion that they should not be developed at all, at least not until some time in the future. Ottawa might well take such a view.
I should like to support the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) in his endeavour to have the level raised from $250,000 to $500,000. In this age of inflation we shall hardly have time to turn around before this figure of $250,000 is obviously inapplicable. If, as is estimated, it is costing between $50,000 and $100,000 to provide employment for one worker, then this figure of $250,000 means we are looking at a firm with three or four employees. I think this is one area, if the bill is to find any acceptance in the country, that we should look at very carefully.

I refer to the Shaheen development in that province which has often been described as one of our economically poorer provinces. There has been an attempt by a misguided federal government to assist that province in economic development. This particular project was directed toward a federal-provincial port service development which would be to the benefit of one privately owned foreign corporation. I should like to ask, who was to receive the benefits of this development, and who was to provide the risk? We do not know as yet who would benefit in the long run, but in terms of profits they will all go to the company.
Let me conclude this series of examples by pointing out one essential and logical point. It is important for the federal government to assume a national responsibility in respect of foreign ownership so that we do not leave the provinces of Canada, particularly the poorest, in a position where they have to go out in competition with each other for badly needed jobs, at the taxpayers' expense and to the benefit of private investors.

Those who do not agree with my argument will have the opportunity to reply. Foreign ownership in this industry results in the loss of hundreds of millions of dollars in profits and the loss of many hundreds of thousands of jobs. Much of our petroleum industry has been owned for many years by investors in the United States, in England and in The Netherlands. Let me point out to hon. members that Supertest, which was one of the few Canadian-owned companies, was taken over by the British Petroleum Company which is owned by foreign investors and controlling interest is held by the government of Great Britain. I should like to ask hon. members who are those who receive the benefits of that operation in Canada?
Another point I should like to make is this. Because of the foreign ownership of these petroleum companies, the research and development done by young scientists is done by young Englishmen, Americans and Dutchmen rather than by young Canadians. I suggest this is a second negative consequence that results from foreign ownership.
A third point I should like to mention is the fact that because of interests owned by people abroad, the benefits of associated activities in the petrochemical and plastics industries are in effect exported from Canada, and particularly from Alberta. It is not the people of Alberta or the people of southern Ontario, where most of the manufacturing in this country takes place, that benefit from this research and development: the people who receive the benefits of secondary or associated industries are not the people of Alberta or the people of Canada, but the people of Great Britain, Holland and the United States.
Let me point out a third negative consequence of private development of the natural resources of Alberta. The hon. member for Crowfoot talked about doing the same thing in respect of the tar sands as we have done for the rest of petroleum development in the province of Alberta. I suggest to him that the time has come to stop future foreign development of our petroleum industry. We must take this development out of the hands of the private sector and we must take it out of the hands, particularly, of the foreign-owned private sector.
I conclude the point by saying that he could not have selected a better industry in this country to condemn his own case than the petroleum industry of Alberta. The policy of this party is that the future development of the tar sands must depend, not exclusively on the federal government-because the control of resources is within provincial jurisdiction-but on joint federal-provincial public control of the tar sands development so that in terms of future profits we will stop their export, we will keep the research in Canada and the secondary industry will then be built up in Canada and for Canadians, not for

people who live elsewhere, so that Canadians and not others will get the prime benefits of our natural heritage.
I conclude by saying that the Tory amendments, if accepted, would vitiate a reasonable proposal-not one that we think will be hallowed in the socialist heavens in the years hereafter, but a measure that goes some way in the right direction. Anyone who can conceivably take that Tory position must be someone who really does not care at all about the future of the economic independence of this country.

The minister addressed his remarks to the amendments presented by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). I will deal first with amending motions Nos. 2, 5 and 6. They represent the legitimate concerns of the provincial governments. Those legitimate concerns were expressed before the committee by all of the provinces that appeared, including the provinces that approved this bill.
I want to remind the minister of the representations made by the province of Ontario when presenting its views on the bill. In essence, the province of Ontario said, "Yes, we need some bill controlling foreign ownership, but there must be close consultation between the federal and provincial governments in the review process". That brief from the province of Ontario also stressed:
The federal government provide the province in which the foreign investment is proposed with a copy of the notification and any additional information submitted by the foreign investor.
The provinces be provided with full opportunity to submit their views on proposed investments.
The federal government inform the provinces of any additional details concerning the criteria which will be used in the review process...
It is also evident that the consideration of provincial viewpoints provides for a regional dimension to foreign investment policy in
[Mr. Blenkarn.)
Canada. Ontario recognizes that the administration of the proposed act must be sensitive to diverse provincial viewpoints. However, the wider interventionist role which will be available to the federal government should not be used as an instrument of regional development policy. In our view, the objective of reducing regional disparities should be pursued through programs which have been directly designed for this purpose ...
It is of serious concern to Ontario that there be clarification of the manner in which the federal government proposes to ascertain the nature and status of provincial policy objectives for the purposes of the review process.
The minister was present. The province of Ontario thoroughly approved a review process, but at the same time it expressed serious concern. I would point out that amendments Nos. 2, 5 and 6 are proposed by a member from another province, one that sometimes is said to be a depressed province that needs additional regional assistance. I wish to point out that we have had a number of speakers in support of the amendments, one being a member representing the province of Alberta, a province that certainly cannot be termed a depressed province.
The problem is that Canada is composed of regions. Canada is a vast nation. It has great scope, and these amendments will allow for recognition of that scope. They do not destroy the quality of the bill. They do not mean a provincial veto, not by any means. They really mean that the government must consult with the provinces on whether foreign investment is to be allowed or rejected or whether foreign takeover is to be allowed or rejected. They provide for consultation with the provinces directly affected. The minister knows that this is the position of his party.
From the experiences this House has witnessed over past weeks, the minister should know how much a province in this country can really trust the federal government. Members of the government of Alberta were in Ottawa a week ago yesterday. They thought they had a deal with the government. The government does not consult through the normal process. Its attitude towards consultation is demonstrated in the issuance of press releases and the making of speeches.
Members of the federal government do not want to talk. They do not want to consult. The course of events in connection with the oil issue over past weeks has demonstrated that the regions of this country really cannot rely on the Ottawa bureaucracy to protect the national interest of Canada. It is only in that vein that we proposed these amendments and in which I recommend them to this House.
This was a very serious issue before the committee, Mr. Speaker. The representatives of the province of Quebec who appeared were also concerned. I suggest to hon. members on the other side, who come from that province, that they should look seriously at these amendments and not be too bound by the whip, but be bound by their consciences for the good of Canada and the good of their regions.
I shall move on to the question of threshold limits at this point, but I may want to come back to the other issues. The hon. member for Crowfoot proposed a capital limit of half a million dollars instead of the $250,000
November 6, 1973

capital limit suggested in the bill. This House has been in receipt of two bills in this session dealing with increases in the old age pensions, which I suppose were totally brought about by inflation. We have recently dealt on second reading with amendments to the Canada Pension Plan. Some of the most expressed concerns in settling the railway strike this year arose because of the effect of inflation on railway workers.
When this bill was conceived some three years ago, $250,000 may have appeared to be quite realistic. But with the incidence of inflation, the incidence of growth and the fact that this government has increased the money supply in Canada by 50 per cent in the last three years, that cannot now be considered a realistic figure. To suggest a capital limit of $500,000 today is probably to say exactly what was intended by the authors of the bill when it was proposed to the government some years ago. I think the House should look at the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Crowfoot because it makes sense.
I should like to draw to the attention of the minister the suggestions he made in committee when dealing with the bill. At that time he said he did not anticipate the creation of a new, enlarged bureaucracy but that we would make use of existing industrial expertise and administrative services. He also said that his guesstimate was that from 15 to 20 officers, and an equivalent number of support staff, is all that would be required. Fifteen or 20 people with equivalent support staff-possibly a total complement of 40 to 50 people, and possibly not even that number are expected to handle this bill?
Does the minister expect that a staff of that size could look after every takeover involving corporations having only $250,000 in gross assets? I would remind the House of the minister's statement this afternoon when he said that $250,000 in gross assets may mean $5,000, $10,000 or $20,000 in real capital, with the rest in debt capital. Mr. Speaker, it is a pretty small company that has gross assets of $250,000 in this age. Surely we cannot expect 15 or 20 officers and the equivalent number of support staff to review investments to the low threshold level of $250,000-especially in this age of liberal inflation.
Amendment No. 3 was proposed by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). The hon. member has not had much experience in business and he really does not understand that the gross turnover of $3 million proposed in the bill is not very high. His suggestion to reduce that amount to $1.5 million is totally ridiculous. As I have stated already in connection with the capital amount, if the bill were amended to limit gross turnover to $1.5 million, we would have to hire a veritable army to administer it.
Some hon. members who have already spoken tonight have suggested that this party is against the foreign takeover bill. I deny that categorically and would remind you, Sir, that this party has always been the national party of Canada. This party is the party of Macdonald who made this country. This party is the party of Borden who in 1911 held this country together. And in recent history this is the party that stood and laid a flag across a bench in this House and said something about a pipeline that those fellows gave away!

Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members of the House for allowing me to continue. I will try not to bore them or the minister. Let me refer again to what he said in committee. The minister went on to say that for small Canadian companies there is a great big limit. They only need to pay 25 per cent, or half the corporate tax rate, until they earn $50,000 in one year. He neglected to say that under the old Income Tax Act small companies had to pay a low rate of tax on the first $35,000 of earnings. That rate would go on and on, and was designed to allow companies to build up their position. Under the current act, the reduced allowance for small businesses ceases after a

November 6, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act business has earned a gross of $400,000 or $50,000 each year for eight years. So when we get down to it, what encouragement has the government given for Canadians to invest?
The government introduced a capital gains tax. It applies to Canadians but does not apply to Americans. Americans can still invest in Canada; they do not pay the Canadian capital gains tax. What did it do about the withholding tax? It said that it would increase it to 25 per cent for foreigners, but it did not renegotiate tax treaties with most favoured nations. As a result, foreigners can come in, take their profits home and only pay 15 per cent.
The government did not follow the Carter commission's recommendations with respect to income tax. It had said that income tax would rise to a maximum of 50 per cent and never go beyond that. It said, as well, that corporate and personal income taxes should be integrated. Those to my left went on and on asking for that. But no, the government did not do that. It made sure that income taxes continued to rise to the 60 per cent level. There was no integration of corporate and personal taxes. Oh, yes, one can see that it is great at holding out incentives-but let us consider a few other things. My leader suggested in the last election, and perhaps the government will implement this, that people who want to buy shares in small businesses should be able to deduct the cost of those shares from income. The government did not support that proposal. Actually, it called the proposal ridiculous. After all, it does not want little people to own businesses in Canada.
There was a further suggestion for an arrangement under which interest on personal loans could be deducted, or applied against business expenses, or the cost of investing in a small business. But this government will not go for that-it will not help Canadians invest in Canada. It was also suggested that banks should be required to give preferred treatment to Canadian borrowers. What is the truth of the matter? How many Canadian corporations are given the prime rate? How many Canadian corporations must go to the government's own agency, the IDB, and pay 12 per cent or 13 per cent for money?
Really, Sir, we are governed by a government that is totally negative. The government does not want to give Canadians a break; it is not interested in building Canada. This government says "thou shalt not"-and that is the total concept behind this bill. We need a total program which will encourage Canadians to be masters of their own house. If Canada is to develop as a nation, it cannot be governed by a government whose only policy is "No."

When I was first elected to this House, I must confess that I did not consider the question of foreign ownership and foreign takeover as being extremely serious. However, having listened to a number of hon. members for whom I have great respect-and that does not include the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie)-I have learned that there really is some difficulty in this country with respect to foreign ownership.
I can read statistics as well as the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, and I can see that there is a problem in Canada. The major industries of this country are to a great extent owned by foreigners. I am convinced that we must make an assault on that problem within the next few years. However, we will not make that assault if we use the tools of negativism. That assault will not be undertaken successfully if we merely say, as the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) suggested, "Thou shalt not do these things".
The government can do certain things. My party says that this is a negative bill because it only attacks one half of the problem. The bill does nothing with respect to the other half of the problem, which involves the question of incentives, the limiting of unemployment, the lessening of the rate of inflation which disturbs people, the creation of new financial institutions, and the implementation of policies which will assist us in our drive to create secondary industry in this country which is Canadian owned. All these things ought to be done. This bill does little to bring these things about. These improvements will not be brought about because the bill does not create the right atmosphere for them. That is our difficulty with this bill.

Mr. Speaker, the study of Bill C-132 has been very much delayed. Now that the harm has been done, that foreigners have strong control over our business in Canada, it is difficult to make them go back and any such law will never have much utility.
To prevent that the same harm will be done to our national economy in the future, this bill will perhaps stop small foreign firms from setting up in Canada, unless it is to our benefit that they be invited or accepted. However, the existing great corporations will always manage one way or the other to prosper at their normal rate among our Canadian firms.
Small fines of $10,000 will not deter them from continuing their activities.
Bill C-132 contains enough loopholes to let things go on as they are, while allowing us to tell everyone that we now have a legislation protecting Canadian capital and forbidding foreign capital to enter the country unless it is recognized and proven to be of benefit to us.
Mr. Speaker, no need to be very smart to realize that the $10,000 fine could discourage small businesses, but not large ones, from risking their coming here, so that we can consider the legislation to bring further protection to big capital already invested in the country, since it prevents new competition from taking root.
In the long run, the legislation is justifiable in the sense that it will stop foreigners from making new investments, but on the other hand, it will let the capital already invested here expand without any obstacle or penalty.
If we look quickly at the billions of dollars in foreign capital already invested in Canada, can we still state that the legislation brought about by Bill C-132 will stop General Motors from expanding and developing in Canada for

So there you have about fifty of the great companies whose capital is wholly or partially foreign, and they are all taking advantage of our natural resources, of a mostly Canadian labour force, and especially of our customers, our purchasing power and our savings, whenever that suits them, when shares are sold on the market.
Mr. Speaker, those are facts we must accept. In the same way, we have to accept foreign capital, whether we like it or not. It is already done, no matter who was responsible for it. Is that what we want to change through the so-called legislation before us today, Bill C-132? Is it those companies we want to hurt? Do we really want those companies to pay $10,000 fines? Will those firms be affected by this minor legislation that we are throwing in their way? One can very well see that it is mere window dressing for the benefit of those who are yapping against the influx of foreign capital in our corporations. But, if we truly want foreign capital to work for Canadians we should not throw it out nor prevent it from coming to help us because if we really need capital and if we do not know how to produce it we must go right at the source of this capital so necessary for our industrial development and our national economy.
If ever we truly want foreign capital to work in this country for Canadians while ensuring reasonable profits to its owners, even a foreign owner, we shall have better things to do than raising small inconveniences as we are trying to do through Bill C-132.
We will not even need to pass new laws to this effect. We will just have to take a hard look at our tax system which, generally speaking, gives too much protection to

corporate capital to the prejudice of income earned through the work of Canadians and even to the prejudice of the purchasing power of Canadians who must pay too much for the goods and services required for their wellbeing so that corporate profits may be higher whether they stem from Canadian or foreign capital.
Once the government will have decided to render justice to all Canadians whether they be self-employed, unionized or in partnerships, whether they be organized as corporations of any kind, then it will be worthwhile to speak about national economic balance between people, families and corporations and then there will be no question of treating foreign capital differently from Canadian capital because it will always be welcome, will no longer be evil and will be profitable to all Canadians.
Generally speaking, Canadians do not complain about foreign capital which is the basis of our national economy. In fact, the issue is not where it is coming from. The issue is to have capital when you need it. We should not be scared when things go wrong somewhere. Foreign capital is not always to be blamed, neither is our international trade. But we are trying to say that if things are turning out badly it is not our fault. That is the trouble. Nobody wants to take his responsibilities. We refuse to admit that if things go wrong, we too could have contributed to such a state of affairs.
And if we are responsible, it becomes much easier to correct such a situation than to pretend that it is someone else's fault. Instead of always blaming others for our dissatisfaction, let us finally recognize that we have caused it and let us shoulder our responsibilities. Let us correct what is within our reach here, in Parliament. The whole taxation system was under consideration for a great many years and with what results? Under the pretence of levying heavier taxes on large companies, of taxing capital gains, these companies are realizing ever larger profits, accumulating more and more reserves each year; prices never cease to go up everywhere precisely in order to let the companies obtain higher profits and get in more reserves. This is why, despite improved production each year in Canada, our governments run deeper into debt, show ever increasing deficits. People are desparate because of rising prices, but companies are progressing, capitalizing and taking further advantage of the inertia of our government which cares little about the stability of the Canadian economy. It is not important if the capital is supplied by our people or by foreigners; the trouble is not there. But they do not want to see what is wrong. It is the unfair distribution of taxes among individuals and corporations that is wrong; individuals are always Canadian workers, but the capital of corporations may be Canadian or foreign but anyway, this capital is always protected, non-taxable, privileged, encouraged by all kinds of allowed and non taxable reserves.
It is not because the capital is foreign or Canadian that companies are not properly taxed as compared with individuals, but because they are not taxed. Therefore, it would be sufficient to tax them properly, not more than individuals, but equally, that is to say in proportion to their profits.
Besides, Mr. Speaker, are dividends paid on share capital of foreign-owned companies as important as that? Must

If we consider the facts, we will see that dividends paid on foreign capital are very small and that we must not hold them responsible for our economic troubles.
If we look at statistics in this country, we see that out of a production of $103 billion in 1972, the year that ended last March, only $874 million were paid to non-residents, whether from the United States or other countries. Therefore, $874 million out of $103 billion, in 1972, do not even represent 1 per cent of our whole production that goes to foreign countries in purchasing power, under the form of dividends paid on share capital of foreign-owned corporations.
