subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-DISCONTINUANCE OF VETERANS LAND ACT BENEFITS-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION-REASON FOR ACTION
VETERANS AFFAIRS-DISCONTINUANCE OF VETERANS LAND ACT BENEFITS-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION-REASON FOR ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought I was in second position tonight, but I guess I am first. I have had the chance of glancing up at the press, and since the question that I have put forward is about veterans affairs they can all have a ten-minute sleep.
I again make representation to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) to try to impress upon him the need to reconsider the phasing out of the Veterans Land Act. In my question to him I mentioned the fact that there are 125,000 veterans who are certified at the present and must make application for loan before March, 1974. I understand that this figure is now approaching 140,000 veterans who qualify for certification and must apply before March, 1974.
It is my understanding, also, that the Veterans Land Act administration expects that only 5 per cent of these 140,000 will come forward. From what I can gather, the department's answer to the question as to why so many veterans have not come forward is that this is because many veterans merely made sure they obtained certification before October, 1968, in the event that they might want to apply for loans. This may be so in some cases, but to my mind, judging from the many letters and grievances arriving in my office-and I am sure this is true of other hon. members-the Veterans Land Act, even with the many amendments brought in over the years, has not kept pace with the changing conditions, particularly with the situation which exists at this time.
For example, under part II of the Veterans Land Act it is provided that veterans can borrow up to $18,000. Everyone who has remained here tonight knows it is impossible to build a home for that amount or, for that matter, even to build a basement. I contend that if the act had been amended to meet inflationary costs, many thousands of veterans would now be taking advantage of their qualification.
Furthermore, a more serious restriction is the lot requirement of one-half an acre. In some cases this can be reduced by 20 per cent. Everyone knows that not only veterans but every citizen in Canada who wants to build a house is burdened with the cost of land which denies him the opportunity of acquiring a home for himself and his family. In this respect the government has failed to meet changing conditions, to the detriment of the war veteran.
With regard to the deadline date for certification of October 1, 1968, it is difficult for me to understand the adamant position the department is taking in stating that
November 6, 1973

everyone has had an opportunity to apply before that date. The minister knows there are many veterans who, through circumstances beyond their control, were not knowledgeable of the deadline date and are being denied their rights under the charter. This is true even though the minister states that everyone was aware of the situation.
It is worth while mentioning the answer given by the minister in which he stated that we have no right to deviate from the legislation as it now stands. Nothing, to my mind, is farther from the fact. If I had the time I could relate the literally thousands of amendments brought forth since 1920 when the act was known as the Soldier Settlement Act. The amount of the loans has been amended time and time again because of the increase in costs, and lot requirements have been amended from time to time.
If ever there was a time when it would be sensible to lift the deadline for certification, it is now when the housing crisis which exists in Canada was never more acute. The National Housing Act as it exists, with all its improvements, cannot meet the needs of low-income Canadians. We have the machinery already existing under the Veterans Land Act to fill the needs of many thousands of veteran Canadian citizens to whom the government made a commitment many years ago when the then prime minister of the country said, in 1917, that no Canadian would ever be able to say that the government of the day would not fulfil its obligation to the veterans who served their country.
Now, the government of today is reneging on the commitments it made back in 1917. The government can remove the deadline dates, they can increase the amount of loans, and they can reduce the lot requirements by simple amendments; also, they can remove the restrictions on deadline dates. I am sure the minister would want to do this-but instead he is listening to his cabinet colleagues who are denying the veterans their right. Such action cannot be condoned under any circumstances. I hope the minister will tell me why this is being done.

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-DISCONTINUANCE OF VETERANS LAND ACT BENEFITS-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION-REASON FOR ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in considering representations to extend the statutory deadline of March 31, 1974, for qualified veterans to submit loan applications under the Veterans Land Act, it is essential to look at the matter in the perspective of the purpose of the act and its alternative relationship to other rehabilitation measures.
As indicated in previous statements which I have made both in the House and to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, VLA was not designed as a program of urban housing nor as part of a retirement program for persons reaching the end of their productive careers. Its basic purpose was to provide loans for the purchase of agricultural land to be used on a full or part time farming basis by veterans who were interested in this form of rehabilitation program on their return to civilian life following wartime active force service.
It was recognized that many veterans would neither wish nor find it practical to settle under the Veterans Land Act. Two other programs were enacted: university training under the Veterans Rehabilitation Act, and reestablishment credits under the War Service Grants Act.
Adjournment Debate
The benefits under all three programs were alternative one to the other. Each veteran had the right to choose whichever plan he considered would best serve his needs and desires. The department's university training program was concluded in the 1950s, and October 31, 1968, was the final date for veterans to use re-establishment credit benefits. As I have mentioned previously in the House, virtually every veteran who writes to me about VLA has used either of the other two alternative benefits.
Having regard for the basic purpose of the Veterans Land Act and its alternative relationship to the other two measures, in 1965 parliament established deadlines to phase out VLA lending operations in a reasonable and orderly manner. By next March, almost 30 years will have elapsed since the end of World War II, and 20 years in the case of the Korean conflict. In the context of a rehabilitation measure to assist veterans to pick up the threads of civilian life following wartime active service, I suggest those genuinely interested in land settlement assistance will have had ample time to find properties suitable for this purpose.
Reference was made to the fact that some 125,000 veterans-I think the hon. member said 140,000-who hold VLA qualification certificates have not applied for VLA benefits. I am satisfied that the vast majority of these veterans simply took the precaution of obtaining such a certificate by the deadline of October 31, 1968. Those with a sincere interest in being established on the land have been settled in the intervening five years or are taking steps to do so before the end of March, 1974.
I have received some representations that March 31, 1974, is premature for qualified veterans still serving in the armed forces. I would like to mention that many such veterans are already established under the act and that others are in the process of doing so. The existing terms of the legislation are sufficiently flexible to accommodate these veterans.
In summary, I believe the terminal dates established by parliament more than eight years ago for the orderly phase out of VLA lending operations were reasonable and realistic at the time and remain so today. By next March approximately 140,000 veterans will have been settled, involving an investment of public funds of more than $1.25 billion. Those are impressive totals, and, I suggest, reflect full attainment of the purposes of this alternative rehabilitation measure as contemplated by the framers of the legislation.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-POSSIBILITY OF INCREASE IN WAGE OFFER TO NORTHWEST TERRITORIES NURSES BECAUSE OF WORKING CONDITIONS AND COST OF LIVING-DANGER PAY
PUBLIC SERVICE-POSSIBILITY OF INCREASE IN WAGE OFFER TO NORTHWEST TERRITORIES NURSES BECAUSE OF WORKING CONDITIONS AND COST OF LIVING-DANGER PAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I again wish to raise the matter of pay awards to nurses in Canada's northern territories, which are inadequate almost any way you look at them. I hope the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) will not hesitate to reopen negotiations with this group of people who could have chosen the right to strike as a means of contract dispute settlement, but instead opted for arbitration. Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
November 6, 1973
Adjournment Debate
Speaker, the nurses are dissatisfied and insulted by the award of the arbitration tribunal.
Nurses at our northern hospitals and nursing stations have been offered a 6 per cent increase at a time when the national cost of living has increased by 8.2 per cent. The cost of living in Inuvik is 68 per cent higher than in the prairie provinces, where the basic wage rates for nurses are higher. In Norman Wells the cost of living is 98 per cent higher. I would like to point out to the President of the Treasury Board and those working under him that the isolation post allowance is ridiculously inadequate to cover this gap.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to outline some of the extra responsibilities facing northern nurses to which nurses in the south are generally not exposed. Nursing stations in remote northern areas have no physician nearby and the nurses must often assume responsibilities normally handled by doctors. Sometimes they must escort very ill patients from small settlements to hospitals in the larger communities, and sometimes on to Edmonton. These emergency flights are often hazardous, especially in the winter, and as a pilot I know about the fog and icing conditions that occur, the poor landing strips, and so on. Ten per cent danger pay would not seem an unreasonable demand.
A patient's condition has often been known to change in flight, again requiring special responsibility on the part of the nurse. Northern nurses have had to deliver babies and relieve haemorrhaging patients while in flight in a little Cessna 185. They have to put up with unruliness on the part of psychotics who are to be evacuated. These nurses work long hours. They are under 24-hour standby. They are often shortstaffed, and they must sometimes live in a confined environment. Surely increased sick leave and vacation leave are called for.
The nurses of the Canadian north are required to have two years training besides their high school diplomas. Their work requires heavy responsibility and high professional responsibility. They must work with human life. And what basic wage is the government offering them? Four dollars an hour-only 20 cents an hour more than full-time postal clerks. Their basic wage is to be raised 6 per cent to $7,800 per annum. At the same time, registered nurses in British Columbia receive over $8,000 a year. Auxiliary dental assistants, who require less schooling, get over $9,000.
For their 24-hour standby, nurses at the nursing stations get only 1V& days off per month. Hospital nurses are on 24-hour call for emergency cases, for which the compensation is $1.50 for eight hours, which works out to about 19 cents an hour. Nineteen cents an hour, Mr. Speaker! How can this be considered a responsible rate of compensation? Obviously it cannot.
Of course, under these conditions it is little surprise that the nurses, only a small number of whom are hired locally, do not see fit to stay on for any length of time in the north. Only four nurses currently on staff at the Inuvik hospital have more than one year's service there. It ends up costing the government more money to bring in new nurses than it would cost to give them some incentive to stay. This I consider to be a most deplorable situation.

Hon. Daniel <J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs): Mr. Speaker, the minister is, of course, concerned to minimize the exposure to hazards of all public servants whether they are employed in the north or at the many locations where there are federal government installations across this country. The government, as employer, has issued many safety standards and guidelines in the last two or three years and the safety of public servants is under constant examination by staff at Treasury Board and, of course, by departments who in the final analysis have the responsiblity for the proper and safe deployment of their staffs.
A number of departments, including the Department of Transport, are jointly studying at this very time new policies affecting travel by public servants in chartered aircraft, particularly with regard to isolated areas. At least one department, which deploys its personnel in isolated areas, has already issued interim guidelines for field operations in the north. The government, as employer, puts its emphasis on the means of reducing to acceptable mini-mums the hazards to which public servants are exposed.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN RESEARCH INTO PROTEIN PRODUCTION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
AGRICULTURE-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN RESEARCH INTO PROTEIN PRODUCTION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 20, as recorded in Hansard at page 5833, I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) the following question:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. Because of the high cost of protein, and in view of the fact that Canada could rectify this problem and become self-sufficient in protein production, is the minister now prepared to authorize more money for research into high protein crops and the elimination of thiglucoside in rapeseed?
The minister replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, we have research programs in this respect. As I said before, I believe, to some hon. members of this House, I think we are doing more in this field than any other country and plan on doing even more.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the only part of the answer I am satisfied with is the part which states "and plan on doing even more". If Canadian agriculture is to go on feeding the millions of people in the world, improved agricultural research programs must be given more attention. The minister has consistently maintained that his department's research programs are second to none in comparison with what other countries are doing. I question the validity of this statement. However, whether or not it is true, what really matters is whether we are concentrating our efforts in the proper directions and making the optimum use of the talent and facilities available to us.
I maintain that the universities of this country have those talents and facilities available and can propel our research efforts in the proper direction. In recent years Canada's universities have been receiving a smaller and smaller percentage of the research funds available for agriculture. It has now reached the point of being ridiculous, for they are receiving only 1 per cent, that is, $600,000 of a $62 million budget, of those moneys allotted for agricultural research in Canada.
Where are all these funds going? Apparently they are being funnelled into that grey area known as the Depart-
November 6, 1973

ment of Agriculture research branch, there to be used for some unco-ordinated, nondescript activities, sometimes totally unrelated to the immediate needs of Canadian farmers.
A well known and respected Canadian scientist, Dr. P. D. MacTaggart-Cowan, has stated that it was the policy of the federal Department of Agriculture to monopolize millions of dollars and as a result starve research scientists at universities. It has long been my belief that a university professor can guide and direct as many as 35 research technicians or students toward a specific goal. At the moment most universities are lucky to have one technician for each professional on staff. University research departments are dependent on outside financing in the form of annual grants to maintain their programs. Because of this dependence on annual grants, permanent staff is very difficult to find and to keep. The best people just will not accept positions which offer small salaries and little personal security.
The biggest problem of university research today is permanent staff. As a result of this we have a definite problem of ineffective utilization of professional university people. There is, in spite of the budget, a lack of research funds in western Canada. This is evident not only at CDA research stations but universities as well. Take rapeseed for example: the project at Saskatoon is inadequately funded. In view of the protein shortage experienced this year, we should be pushing ahead at all costs to eliminate glucosinolate in rapeseed. However, I find that the research presently going on is concentrated on the Argentine variety and not the Polish variety which is best suited to the prairie region.
Besides this, I believe there are only six people working on such research. We should be encouraging universities to test new types of soil, climate, etc., for selection reasons. Even considering all this, I find that research in diseases of rapeseed has not yet got off the ground. To my astonishment, I find that the department is taking pride in building new buildings at Charlottetown, Fredericton and now at Lethbridge instead of using existing facilities or improving facilities at universities. I might add that the Alberta government is now stepping into the field in recognizing the problem and is at least guaranteeing the universities of Alberta some technical staff.
Now I shall address myself to protein self-sufficiency. Although I realize that research is being conducted in Ottawa and Winnipeg in regard to Hiproly barley, I suggest that it seems to take the initiative of western hog growers, of the Alberta Hog Marketing Board and of the province of Alberta in order to get research off the ground of any consequence with regard to high protein, high lysin barley. This is so particularly in the province of Alberta,
Adjournment Debate
the chief red-meat producing and barley producing province of Canada. And we probably have not begun any research into the use of high protein oats. Groat protein in concentrations of between 23 and 25 per cent has been tested at Iowa State University.
My contention, Sir, is that much more could be done by concentrating research on immediate needs and using university expertise, instead of wasting money on nice buildings and government research hierarchy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leopold Corriveau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN RESEARCH INTO PROTEIN PRODUCTION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister shares the concern of the hon. member for the cost of proteins and other agricultural inputs.
As regards proteins, I can reassure the House by saying that Canada produces more vegetable proteins than it needs for its livestock.
The hon. member has referred to the need for protein research, and it would be appropriate to mention a few aspects of the present studies. Among the most interesting developments, we can mention those relating to the reproduction of soya beans and of oats and feed wheat with a higher protein value, as well as the permanent research projects 'supported by the federal government at the University of Manitoba concerning the Faba bean (field-bean).
The department is achieving excellent genetic results concerning glucosilanates in rapeseed, and production of a variety of rapeseed with a low glucosilanate content is expected by 1975. This means simply that we then expect to get into commercial production a variety of rapeseed the oilcake from which will be used much more extensively and with a far greater flexibility than that of varieties now in use. The main restriction in all this research has to do, however, with the reproduction rate.
Through the use of hothouses and other technical means, it is possible to get two crops a year, thus reducing considerably the time required for the development of new varieties. This method has speeded up our discovery of some possibly useful varieties, and by combining these results with reproduction in warmer climates during winter, it was possible to get these useful varieties ready for commercial production in a much shorter period.
The hon. member will no doubt remember the establishment of a $1 million fund for the development of new crops, as well as the granting of an important subsidy for the pilot project concerning a plant for the processing of oil and protein in Saskatchewan.
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for having given me the opportunity of speaking briefly on research concerning feed with a high protein content at the Department of Agriculture.

Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.28 p.m.
